meta.blurb: A thousand years ago the great cities were not in Europe. So why did a few countries get rich first? Historians point to place, rules and chance, and each gets a fair hearing, from the first farms to the first factories.
meta.bible: A single narrator speaks to the reader, curious, fair and clear. Places: Fertile Crescent, Mesopotamia, Uruk (an early city), Levant, Eurasia, Yangtze (river in China), Mexico, Andes, Americas, Africa, New Guinea, Mediterranean, Europe, China, India, Baghdad, Cairo, Kaifeng, Egypt, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Switzerland, Germany, Belgium, France, Spain, Portugal, Caribbean, Atlantic. People (all long dead): Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain in 1492; Vasco da Gama of Portugal reached India in 1498; Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press in Germany about 1450; Thomas Newcomen built a steam pumping engine in 1712; James Watt improved it in the 1760s; Edward Jenner showed vaccination in 1796. Events: the Black Death reached Europe in 1347; the Great Divergence is the widening gap in wealth after about 1800; the Meiji government of Japan began in 1868; the Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 1700s; the first public steam railway opened in 1825. Key terms: Surplus, Teosinte, Sorghum, Taro, Millet, Barley, Granaries, Scribes, Bronze, Plough, Ploughs, Lorries, Ironmonger, Serfs, Locomotives, Smallpox, Measles, Influenza, Cowpox, Vaccine, Vaccination, Malaria, Landlocked, Institutions, Divergence, Colonised, Cobs, Ore, Tin, Copper, Duchies, Clique, Tinkering. Added for the full-length book. Places: Levant, Natufian villages, Kuk, Uruk, Gilgamesh, Tigris, Euphrates, Nile, Giza, Indus Valley, Mohenjo-daro, Caral, Yellow River, Akkad, Babylon, Persia, Lydia, Silk Roads, Kilwa, Mombasa, Timbuktu, Gao, Mali, Constantinople, Toledo, Venice, Genoa, Florence, Mainz, Saxony, Cajamarca, Tenochtitlan, Potosi, Bolivia, Brazil, Saint-Domingue, Haiti, Bristol, Liverpool, Lisbon, Nantes, Manchester, Rhode Island, Seoul, Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Botswana, Mauritius, Kenya, Ghana, Pakistan, Sicily, Black Sea, Berlin. People and peoples: Aztecs, Aztec, Inca, Maya, Quechua, Nahuatl, Polynesian, Swahili, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Prince Henry of Portugal, Bartolomeu Dias (rounded southern Africa in 1488), Ferdinand Magellan and Juan Sebastian Elcano (voyage around the world, 1519 to 1522), Hernan Cortes (Mexico, 1519), Francisco Pizarro and Atahualpa (Peru, 1532), King Hammurabi (about 1750 BCE), Sargon of Akkad, Mansa Musa (pilgrimage 1324), Admiral Zheng He (fleets 1405 to 1433), Martin Luther (1521), King Charles I (executed 1649), William and Mary (1688), Edward III (defaulted in the 1340s), George Stephenson (railway 1825), John Cockerill, Samuel Slater (mill 1790), Edward Jenner, John Snow (1854), Joseph Bazalgette, Louis Pasteur, Robert Koch, Toussaint Louverture, Deng Xiaoping, Matthew Boulton, James Hargreaves, Richard Arkwright, Samuel Crompton, Meiji. Events and dates: the Silk Roads from about 2,100 years ago; the western Roman Empire fell in 476; Spain sent silver from Potosi from 1545; Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833; slavery ended in the United States in 1865 and in Brazil in 1888; the Bill of Rights, 1689; the Bank of England, 1694; the Spanish Armada, 1588; the Great Stink, 1858; smallpox declared wiped out in 1980; India and Pakistan independent 1947; Ghana 1957; seventeen African countries 1960; Singapore independent 1965; China's reforms from 1978; India's reforms from 1991. Key terms added: Columbian Exchange, Cuneiform, Ziggurat, Khipu, Caravel, Astrolabe, Calico, Condenser, Plantations, Middle Passage, Patent, Subsidies, Tariffs, Tsetse, Cottonopolis, Demographic transition, Asian tigers. Voice and tone: curious, balanced and honest about what is still debated; no invented numbers or quotes; slavery and disease treated factually and without gore; never any suggestion that some peoples are less able than others.
chapters: A Head Start in the Soil

beats.scene: Earth seen at night, with some lands bright with lights and others dark
beats.summary: From space at night, some lands blaze with light and others are almost dark.

beats.scene: Two children in different lands, one in a bright classroom and one carrying water
beats.summary: Where a child is born shapes how long and how well that child is likely to live.

beats.scene: A market stall with scales, coins and baskets of fruit and bread
beats.summary: A country is called rich when its people earn and produce a lot on average.

beats.scene: A busy market in an old Asian city, full of silk and spice
beats.summary: It was not always so: a thousand years ago the great cities were not in Europe.

beats.scene: Domes and towers of Baghdad beside a river, with scholars on a library step
beats.summary: Baghdad, Cairo and Kaifeng were among the largest and most learned cities in the world.

beats.scene: A small European village of timber houses and muddy lanes under grey skies
beats.summary: Much of Europe then was poor, with villages, small towns and few large cities.

beats.scene: A traveller stands between a glowing eastern city and a dim western village
beats.summary: The puzzle is why the places that led then were not the places that led later.

beats.scene: A scholar at a desk with a map, a coin and a die
beats.summary: Historians give three kinds of answer: place, rules and chance.

beats.scene: A teacher and mixed group of students stand around a globe, thinking
beats.summary: No answer may claim that any people is born cleverer than another.

beats.scene: Archaeologists brush soil from old pots while a map and charts lie nearby
beats.summary: Historians, archaeologists and economists build the story from evidence, and some parts are still debated.

beats.scene: A small band of hunters walks across open grassland at sunrise
beats.summary: For most of history people lived in small groups of hunters and gatherers.

beats.scene: A band sits around a night fire with stone tools beside them
beats.summary: Fire and tools of stone, bone and wood let hunting bands live almost anywhere.

beats.scene: A line of travellers crosses a grassy plain towards a dry desert
beats.summary: Modern humans spread from Africa across the whole world, reaching Australia and the Americas.

beats.scene: A cave wall with painted horses and bison, lit by a torch
beats.summary: Cave paintings show that people long ago were just as clever and creative as people today.

beats.scene: Hunters share roasted meat and berries while children play
beats.summary: Hunting bands knew nature deeply, owned little and mostly shared what they had.

beats.scene: A great glacier covers a cold, windy valley where mammoths graze
beats.summary: The last ice age made the climate cold, dry and unpredictable, which was hard on farming.

beats.scene: Green hills and a river valley as the last ice melts
beats.summary: About twelve thousand years ago the ice age ended and the world became warmer and steadier.

beats.scene: Natufian people in round stone houses beside a grassy hillside
beats.summary: In the Levant some hunting peoples settled in villages and harvested wild grain before farming began.

beats.scene: Hands cut wild grain with a stone sickle and grind seeds
beats.summary: These people cut wild grain with stone sickles, ground it and stored seeds in pits.

beats.scene: A young woman presses seeds into soil as elders watch
beats.summary: Nobody decided to invent farming; it grew slowly over many generations, and historians still ask why.

beats.scene: Wild wheat and barley glowing gold on dry hills in western Asia
beats.summary: In the Fertile Crescent, wild wheat, barley, peas and lentils were easy to farm.

beats.scene: A farmer holds two ears of grain, one wild and one with fuller seeds
beats.summary: Farmers chose the best seeds each year, and over time the plants changed to suit them.

beats.scene: Farmers wade through green rice fields in southern China at dawn
beats.summary: In China, rice was first farmed in the south and millet in the north.

beats.scene: A Mexican field with maize, beans and squash growing together under bright sun
beats.summary: In Mexico farmers turned a wild grass called teosinte into maize, over thousands of years.

beats.scene: A farmer digs purple potatoes on a steep Andean slope with llamas nearby
beats.summary: In the Andes of South America, farmers grew potatoes and other mountain crops.

beats.scene: Farmers tend tall sorghum and millet beside a river in West Africa
beats.summary: In Africa, people farmed sorghum, millet, African rice and yams, plants their own lands provided.

beats.scene: Farmers tend taro in a misty highland garden in New Guinea
beats.summary: In the highlands of New Guinea people farmed taro, bananas and sugar cane.

beats.scene: A world map with several glowing patches in Asia, Africa and the Americas
beats.summary: Farming began separately in several parts of the world, using different plants.

beats.scene: A thin farmer and a strong hunter stand side by side in a field
beats.summary: Early farming was hard work, and some early farmers were less healthy than hunters, but it fed more people.

beats.scene: Farmers with seed bags walk slowly toward a green, forested land
beats.summary: Farming spread outward from its homelands, slowly, as farmers moved and as ideas travelled.

beats.scene: A village of mud houses beside golden fields, with jars of stored grain
beats.summary: Farming made more food, so people settled in villages and their numbers grew.

beats.scene: A granary door, a farmer with a counting stick, a watchful neighbour
beats.summary: Stored food could be owned, counted, traded and guarded, so wealth and rank began to appear.

beats.scene: A rich field of wheat, rice and maize beside a patch of weeds
beats.summary: Few wild plants make good crops, and only a handful feed most of the world.

beats.scene: A farmer compares a big-seeded wild grass with a tiny-seeded weed
beats.summary: Plants with big, easy seeds became crops; bitter, slow trees such as oaks did not.

beats.scene: A map of western Asia with golden patches and a farmer with seed
beats.summary: The Fertile Crescent had the most useful wild plants and animals, so farming started there early.

beats.scene: A long road across wide fields, with wagons carrying sacks of seed
beats.summary: Eurasia is wide from east to west, so crops could spread across similar climates.

beats.scene: A map of the Americas and Africa marked with mountains, jungle and desert
beats.summary: The Americas and Africa run north to south, with deserts and jungles that slowed the spread of crops.

beats.scene: A land with red soil, eucalyptus trees, and a fish trap in a stream
beats.summary: Australia had few suitable crops, and its peoples built rich ways of life without farming.

beats.scene: Many people at a crowded market: potters, smiths, a weaver and a trader
beats.summary: More people meant more thinkers, makers and traders, and ideas could build on one another.

beats.scene: Broken walls and dry fields where an ancient farming city once stood
beats.summary: A head start is not a guarantee: the old farming lands are not the richest today.

beats.scene: A shepherd watches sheep and goats on a dry hillside
beats.summary: In western Asia people tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs about ten thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A zebra in a grassy field while a farmer holds out a rope
beats.summary: Few wild animals can be tamed: they must be calm, breed in captivity and eat common food.

beats.scene: Two oxen pull a wooden plough across a wide field
beats.summary: Oxen pulled ploughs and carts, so farms grew more food and trade grew.

beats.scene: A woman milks a goat while another spins wool beside a pot of cheese
beats.summary: Animals also gave milk, wool, leather and cheese, and not only meat.

beats.scene: A horse rider and a line of camels cross grass and desert
beats.summary: Horses and camels, tamed later, carried riders and goods across great distances.

beats.scene: A llama carries bundles along a rocky mountain path in the Andes
beats.summary: The Americas had few animals suited to farm work, so there were no ploughs or ox carts.

beats.scene: A child's toy with wheels beside a stone temple in Mexico
beats.summary: Wheels were known in the Americas on toys, but with no big animals to pull them they were not used for carts.

beats.scene: Pigs, ducks and people share a crowded farmyard beside a market stall
beats.summary: Many human diseases began in farm animals, once people lived close to them.

beats.scene: A mother holds a sick child while a healer looks on
beats.summary: Farming peoples suffered many epidemics, and the survivors built up some resistance.

beats.scene: Distant ships on the horizon and a quiet village on the shore
beats.summary: Peoples who had never met these diseases had no protection, which would matter terribly later.

beats.scene: Potters, builders and scribes at work in a busy early city
beats.summary: Surplus food freed some people to become specialists, and towns grew.

beats.scene: Canals carry river water to green fields beneath a hot sun
beats.summary: In Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates, farmers dug canals to bring river water to dry fields.

beats.scene: The tall walls and temple towers of the city of Uruk beside a river
beats.summary: Uruk in Mesopotamia, more than five thousand years ago, was one of the first great cities.

beats.scene: A stepped temple tower called a ziggurat rises above a city of mud-brick houses
beats.summary: Temples were more than places of worship: they stored grain and managed work and wages.

beats.scene: A potter's wheel, a weaver's loom and a trader with balance scales
beats.summary: City workshops made pots on wheels, woven cloth and metal goods that were traded far away.

beats.scene: Pyramids rise beside the Nile as workers drag huge stones on wooden sleds
beats.summary: Egypt grew rich along the Nile, whose yearly flood fed the farms, and its kings built great pyramids.

beats.scene: A tidy brick city with straight streets, drains and a great bath
beats.summary: In the Indus Valley, cities such as Mohenjo-daro had straight streets and drains.

beats.scene: A map showing early cities in China, Peru and Mexico with small glowing dots
beats.summary: Early cities and states also grew in China, in Peru and in Mexico, quite independently.

beats.scene: A rich ruler in fine cloth watches thin workers carry baskets of earth
beats.summary: Cities were unequal places, where rulers and priests lived far better than workers.

beats.scene: An official with a staff stands between a crowd and a grain store
beats.summary: Cities needed order and records, which would lead to writing, laws and rulers.

beats.scene: A clerk presses small clay tokens into a tablet beside sacks of grain
beats.summary: Writing began about 5,300 years ago in Mesopotamia as a way to count grain, beer and sheep.

beats.scene: A scribe presses a reed into a wet clay tablet
beats.summary: Scribes wrote wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform with a reed, and learned the craft in school for years.

beats.scene: Three writers: one with a brush, one carving stone, one with a reed
beats.summary: Writing was invented independently in Egypt, China and Mexico, and probably in Mesopotamia too.

beats.scene: A king receives rolled scrolls and clay tablets from kneeling officials
beats.summary: Writing made laws, contracts, letters and stories possible, and let knowledge outlast the people who held it.

beats.scene: A ruler's officials count sacks of grain while soldiers march in line
beats.summary: Rulers built states: they collected taxes, made laws and raised armies.

beats.scene: A tall stone pillar covered in writing stands before a king and a crowd
beats.summary: About 3,750 years ago King Hammurabi of Babylon had laws carved on a stone for everyone to read.

beats.scene: A king in a chariot and a line of soldiers with spears
beats.summary: Strong states raised armies and conquered their neighbours, building the first empires.

beats.scene: Horse riders carry sealed letters along a stone road past a tower
beats.summary: A large empire needed roads, officials and messengers to hold it together.

beats.scene: A cord with many knots hangs beside an Inca official
beats.summary: The Inca had no writing, but kept records with knotted cords called khipu.

beats.scene: A farmer hands a sack of grain to an official beside a granary
beats.summary: States brought order and public works, but also taxes, forced labour and war.

beats.scene: A smith pours glowing bronze into a stone mould
beats.summary: Bronze, made of copper and tin, gave harder tools and weapons about five thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A caravan carries heavy ingots of tin across rivers and mountains toward a city
beats.summary: Tin was rare, so bronze-making created long trade routes between distant lands.

beats.scene: A farmer with a new iron plough blade breaks hard soil as neighbours watch
beats.summary: Iron, from about 3,200 years ago, was cheaper than bronze, so ordinary people could afford tools.

beats.scene: A Chinese furnace pours molten iron into moulds beneath a tall bellows
beats.summary: Chinese ironworkers were casting iron by about 2,500 years ago, centuries before Europe.

beats.scene: A merchant weighs a small stamped coin against a heavy bag of grain
beats.summary: Coins appeared in Lydia, in Turkey, about 2,600 years ago and made trade much simpler.

beats.scene: Wheat, paper and coins pass between traders on a long caravan road
beats.summary: The Silk Roads linked China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, and carried goods and ideas.

beats.scene: Crops of many kinds in baskets beside a trader with a bag of numbers
beats.summary: Crops and ideas travelled across Eurasia: wheat went east, millet and rice west and south, and Indian numerals spread.

beats.scene: A paper-maker lifts a thin sheet from a vat of pulp
beats.summary: Paper was made in China by about 2,000 years ago, and slowly spread west along the trade routes.

beats.scene: Travellers of many lands gather around a fire at a busy desert inn
beats.summary: Merchants and travellers carried religions, stories and skills as well as goods.

beats.scene: A caravan crosses a bridge and a sick traveller lies in a wagon
beats.summary: Trade also carried danger: diseases travelled along the same roads as goods.

beats.scene: Merchant ships with square sails in a Mediterranean harbour
beats.summary: Water was the cheapest way to move heavy goods, so lands on coasts and rivers traded most.

beats.scene: A map of the Mediterranean ringed by harbours, with sails on the water
beats.summary: The Mediterranean Sea linked many peoples in Europe, Africa and Asia, from Phoenicians to Greeks.

beats.scene: The Roman port of Ostia, with grain ships unloading under a bright sun
beats.summary: The Roman Empire joined the Mediterranean world with roads and sea lanes, and fed Rome with grain from Egypt.

beats.scene: A broken column in a quiet Roman forum with a shepherd
beats.summary: After the western Roman Empire fell in 476, trade and cities shrank in western Europe.

beats.scene: Wooden boats with triangular sails cross the Indian Ocean at sunset
beats.summary: In the Indian Ocean, seasonal monsoon winds let sailors link East Africa, Arabia, India and Asia.

beats.scene: Stone houses and a mosque beside a bay on the coast of East Africa
beats.summary: Swahili trading cities on the East African coast grew rich selling gold, ivory and cloth across the ocean.

beats.scene: A great Chinese ship with many masts and a compass beside the helmsman
beats.summary: In Song China, about a thousand years ago, big ships, the compass and paper money helped trade grow.

beats.scene: A line of camels carries salt and gold across the sandy Sahara
beats.summary: Camel caravans carried gold, salt and cloth across the Sahara, and the kingdom of Mali grew rich.

beats.scene: Polynesian sailors in a double canoe steer by stars across a wide, empty sea
beats.summary: Polynesian sailors crossed thousands of miles of Pacific Ocean using stars, waves and birds.

beats.scene: A glowing web of trade lines over Africa and Eurasia
beats.summary: By about the year 1000, a web of trade joined Asia and Africa, and Europe was at its far edge.

beats.scene: A printing press, a compass and a small cannon on a wooden table
beats.summary: Gunpowder, the compass and printing came from China and were improved in Europe.

beats.scene: A printer pulls a lever on a heavy press as pages dry
beats.summary: About 1450 Johannes Gutenberg built a press with movable metal letters, and books became cheaper.

beats.scene: Many small kingdoms with castles and borders on an old map of Europe
beats.summary: Europe was split into many competing states, divided by mountains, rivers and seas.

beats.scene: Two rival kings in crowns glare at one another across a river border
beats.summary: Rival states competed for money and talent, so ideas that one ruler rejected could find a home with another.

beats.scene: A monk stands before a prince and a crowd in a castle hall
beats.summary: Martin Luther was protected by a German prince in 1521, and printing spread his ideas widely.

beats.scene: A navigator is turned away at the door of a royal court
beats.summary: Christopher Columbus was refused by several courts before Spain agreed to pay for his voyage.

beats.scene: A huge Chinese treasure ship with many masts docks at an African port
beats.summary: China sent giant treasure fleets as far as East Africa from 1405 to 1433, then stopped.

beats.scene: A scholar weighs two scales, one marked peace, one marked freedom
beats.summary: Unity was not simply good or bad: China's one government brought peace and order, but could also stop a good idea.

beats.scene: Italian merchants count coins in a counting house beside a canal
beats.summary: Italian city-states such as Venice and Florence grew rich from trade and banking, and invented better bookkeeping.

beats.scene: A European student copies an Arabic book in a crowded library
beats.summary: Europe learned a great deal from the Islamic world, Byzantium and Asia before it began to lead.

beats.scene: Tall wooden sailing ships leave the Portuguese coast at dawn
beats.summary: Portugal, on Europe's Atlantic edge, sent ships down the coast of Africa step by step from the 1400s.

beats.scene: A small caravel with triangular sails, a compass and star chart on the deck
beats.summary: Better ships, called caravels, and tools such as the compass and the astrolabe made long ocean voyages possible.

beats.scene: A ship rounds a rocky cape in rough seas where two oceans meet
beats.summary: In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa, showing there was a sea route to the east.

beats.scene: Three small ships with the Spanish flag sail into a wide, empty ocean
beats.summary: In 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed west for Spain with three small ships and reached the Caribbean.

beats.scene: A fleet reaches a hot, bustling Indian port beside palm trees and spice sacks
beats.summary: In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached the coast of India for Portugal, after sailing around Africa.

beats.scene: A king's counsellor points at a map of spice islands and a coin chest
beats.summary: Europeans wanted spices, silk and gold, and kings competed for them, but they had little that Asia wanted to buy.

beats.scene: A battered ship with torn sails returns to a Spanish port
beats.summary: In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan set out with five ships; one returned in 1522, having sailed around the world.

beats.scene: A ship with cannon fires on a fortress above a harbour
beats.summary: Portuguese ships with cannon seized ports on the Indian Ocean, such as Goa and Malacca, though they did not conquer big Asian empires.

beats.scene: Soldiers, horses and local allies approach a great island city
beats.summary: In 1519 Hernan Cortes reached Mexico; with thousands of local allies and with disease, he overthrew the Aztec Empire.

beats.scene: A foreign captain and a golden-robed Inca ruler meet in a mountain courtyard
beats.summary: In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa, whose empire was already weakened by disease and civil war.

beats.scene: A quiet, empty village beside a lake in the Americas
beats.summary: European diseases killed millions of people in the Americas.

beats.scene: A family lies sick in a hut while the fields go untended
beats.summary: Epidemics struck whole families at once, so crops went untended and hunger followed.

beats.scene: A scholar with a notebook studies a chart that is only a rough sketch
beats.summary: Historians cannot be sure of the numbers, but most think the population fell by a very large share within a century.

beats.scene: Spanish ships arrive at an empty shore where crops have gone wild
beats.summary: With so many people gone, kingdoms collapsed and Europeans took over empty land and cities.

beats.scene: Miners carry silver ore up a steep mountain beneath a great peak
beats.summary: Silver from mines such as Potosi in the Andes poured into Spain and then into world trade.

beats.scene: A ship holds maize, potatoes, tomatoes and sugar cane bound for Europe and Asia
beats.summary: Plants and animals crossed the oceans in both directions, in what is called the Columbian Exchange.

beats.scene: Farmers dig potatoes from rich soil in a cool northern European field
beats.summary: The potato gave northern Europe a cheap, filling crop, and its population grew.

beats.scene: Farmers in China and Africa harvest sweet potatoes and cassava on terraces
beats.summary: American crops such as maize, cassava and sweet potatoes also fed growing populations in Africa and Asia.

beats.scene: A scale weighs a bag of silver against an empty village
beats.summary: Europe gained land, silver and crops while many Indigenous peoples paid with their lives and lands.

beats.scene: Quechua and Maya families in woven cloth in a mountain market
beats.summary: Indigenous peoples survived: millions of their descendants still speak their languages and keep their traditions today.

beats.scene: Workers in a hot sugar field, with ships waiting at the shore
beats.summary: Sugar, grown on plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean, made huge profits for European traders.

beats.scene: Ships anchor off an African coast as traders and chiefs argue near a fort
beats.summary: When local workers died or fled, planters turned to the Atlantic slave trade, which took people from Africa.

beats.scene: A large ship at anchor off the coast of West Africa at dusk
beats.summary: More than twelve million Africans were forced onto ships and carried across the Atlantic into slavery.

beats.scene: A cramped dark ship's hold with narrow shelves and a single shaft of light
beats.summary: Captives were packed into ships for weeks, with little food or water, and many died on the way.

beats.scene: Rows of enslaved workers cut cane under an overseer while a mill smokes nearby
beats.summary: On plantations, enslaved people worked from dawn to dark with no pay, and the law treated them as property.

beats.scene: Cotton, tobacco, rice and coffee grow in fields under a hot sun
beats.summary: Cotton, tobacco, rice and coffee also depended on enslaved labour in the Americas.

beats.scene: Merchants in a port counting-house toast around a table piled with coin
beats.summary: Slavery and plantation goods made some ports and merchants very rich, and historians still debate how much it helped Europe's economies.

beats.scene: A West African village with empty houses and a fort on a distant hill
beats.summary: The slave trade harmed African societies through lost people and wars, though some kingdoms grew powerful from it.

beats.scene: Free men and women with broken chains celebrate on a hill
beats.summary: In 1791 enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up, and in 1804 Haiti became independent.

beats.scene: A parliament hall with a petition and a ship leaving harbour
beats.summary: Britain ended its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833; the last in the Americas ended in 1888.

beats.scene: A coal mine entrance beside a rain-soaked English town
beats.summary: Britain had coal near the surface and near its ports, which would fuel industry.

beats.scene: A smoky London street in winter with coal carts
beats.summary: As forests were cut down, wood grew scarce and expensive, so people burned coal for heat and for making iron.

beats.scene: A flooded mine shaft with men and horses at a pump
beats.summary: As mines went deeper they flooded, and horse-powered pumps were costly, so there was a need for a better engine.

beats.scene: A steam pumping engine beside a deep mine, with steam rising
beats.summary: Newcomen built a steam pump in 1712, and Watt greatly improved it in the 1760s.

beats.scene: James Watt sketches a new engine beside a small model
beats.summary: James Watt added a separate condenser around 1765, making the engine far more efficient.

beats.scene: Indian cotton cloth printed with flowers beside plain woollen cloth
beats.summary: Indian cotton cloth was prized in Europe, so British makers wanted to copy and beat it.

beats.scene: A wooden spinning machine with many spindles and a young worker beside it
beats.summary: In the 1760s and 1770s, machines such as the spinning jenny and the water frame let one worker spin many threads.

beats.scene: Rows of workers beside clattering spinning machines in a cotton mill
beats.summary: Machines in mills, powered by water and later steam, made cheap cotton cloth, using cotton grown by enslaved people.

beats.scene: A child worker in a dim mill threads a machine
beats.summary: Factory life was hard: long hours, low pay and dangerous machines, with children at work; wages rose only slowly.

beats.scene: Two scholars point at a map of coalfields and a chart of wages
beats.summary: Historians still argue about why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain.

beats.scene: A judge in a wig and two merchants sign a contract in a courtroom
beats.summary: Good rules, such as fair courts and protected property, help people invest.

beats.scene: A king's tax collector seizes a merchant's chest while the merchant pleads
beats.summary: Where rulers could seize property or refuse to repay loans, people hid their wealth and invested less.

beats.scene: A king on a scaffold in a London street, with Parliament behind
beats.summary: In the 1640s a civil war in England ended with the king executed, showing that Parliament would fight for its power.

beats.scene: Lords sign a document in a candlelit hall, with a crown on the table
beats.summary: After 1688, in the Glorious Revolution, Parliament gained real power over the king, which may have made investment safer.

beats.scene: A banker counts notes while a minister holds a ledger of loans
beats.summary: Parliament could be trusted to repay loans, so Britain could borrow cheaply; the Bank of England began in 1694.

beats.scene: A green field with a new hedge and poor villagers watching
beats.summary: Rules did not serve everyone: only a small minority voted, and many poor people lost common land.

beats.scene: An inventor shows a model engine to a clerk with a seal
beats.summary: Patent laws, from 1624, protected inventors' rights for a time, and gave them a reason to share ideas.

beats.scene: Shareholders in a coffee house read a ship list and insure cargo

A1A2: Some countries are very rich, and some countries are very poor.
A child's life can be very different in different countries.

A thousand years ago, the richest lands were not in Europe.
Baghdad was a big, rich city with many books and schools.
At that time, much of Europe was poor and had few big cities.
Why did the rich places change, and why did it happen so late?
Experts give three kinds of answers: place, rules and chance.
No people are born smarter than other people.
Experts study old objects, old maps and old numbers to learn the truth.
For most of history, people lived in small groups and hunted for food.
They used fire to cook food and to keep warm at night.
People walked out of Africa and slowly spread across the world.
Long ago, people painted horses and bison on cave walls.
Hunters knew the land well, and they shared their food.

About twelve thousand years ago, the world became warmer.
In western Asia, some people began to live in villages.
They cut wild grain with stone knives and stored the seeds.
Nobody planned farming, and it grew slowly over many long years.
In western Asia, wild wheat and barley grew on the hills.
Farmers kept the best seeds and planted them again.
In China, people grew rice in the south and millet in the north.
In Mexico, farmers grew corn from a small wild grass.
In the Andes mountains, people grew potatoes on steep slopes.

In New Guinea, people grew taro, bananas and sugar cane.
Farming began in several parts of the world, not just one.
Farming was hard work, but it could feed many people.
Farming slowly spread from place to place over many years.
Farming gave people more food, so villages grew bigger.
Stored grain could be counted, kept and traded.
Only a few plants make good crops for farmers.
Wild wheat has big seeds, and weeds have tiny seeds.
Some lands had more useful plants than other lands.
Crops travelled easily east and west across Asia and Europe.
In the Americas and Africa, crops spread much more slowly.
In Australia, people lived without farming for a very long time.
More people meant more ideas and more people making things.
A head start does not last forever, and many early leaders fell behind.
Long ago, people in Asia tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.
Most wild animals cannot be tamed, even when people try.
Big, strong animals could pull a plough through hard soil.
Farm animals gave people milk, wool and cheese as well.

Living close to animals let new diseases pass to people.
People who got sick and survived became stronger against the disease.

Extra food let some people work at other jobs.
In Mesopotamia, farmers dug canals to bring water to their fields.

The temple kept the city's grain and looked after its people.
City workers made pots, cloth and tools to sell.
In Egypt, farmers grew food beside the great river Nile.

In the first cities, some people were rich and many were poor.
A big city needed rules and records to keep order.

A writer used a reed to make marks in soft clay.
In Egypt, China and Mexico, people also made up writing.
With writing, people could send letters and keep laws.

King Hammurabi had his laws carved on a tall stone.
Strong rulers raised armies and took over weaker neighbours.
Big empires needed roads and messengers to join their lands.
People in the Andes had no writing, but they used knotted cords.
States brought order, but they also took taxes and labour.
Bronze is a strong metal made from copper and tin.
Tin was rare, so traders carried it very far.
Iron was cheaper than bronze, so more people had good tools.
In China, workers made iron tools long before Europe did.
Coins made buying and selling much easier than barter.
Traders carried silk and spices along the long Silk Roads.
Crops and new ideas moved from land to land.
Paper was first made in China, and it spread west very slowly.
On the roads, people shared goods, stories and new ideas.
Trade was useful, but diseases also travelled along the roads.
Moving goods by water was cheaper than moving them by land.
The Mediterranean Sea connected many lands and peoples.
Rome ruled all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea.
When the Roman Empire fell in the west, cities grew smaller.
In the Indian Ocean, sailors rode seasonal winds across the sea.
On the coast of East Africa, rich trading towns grew up.
Chinese ships were large, and sailors used a compass to find the way.
Camels carried gold and salt across the great Sahara desert.
Polynesian sailors crossed the wide Pacific Ocean without maps.
By the year 1000, trade joined Asia, Africa and Europe.
Gunpowder, the compass and printing all began in China.
Gutenberg built a printing press with metal letters in Germany.
Europe was divided into many small kingdoms and cities.
Rival rulers competed with each other, so they needed good ideas.
A prince protected a preacher whom the emperor wanted to punish.
Columbus asked many rulers for ships, and most said no.
China once sent huge fleets to Africa, but then stopped.
One government can bring peace, but it can also stop new ideas.
Italian cities such as Venice grew rich from trade and banking.
Europe learned many things from the Arab and Asian worlds.
Portugal sent ships down the coast of Africa, one trip at a time.
New ships and tools helped sailors to cross the ocean.
In 1488, a Portuguese ship sailed around the south of Africa.
In 1492, Columbus sailed west with three small ships.
In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached India by sea from Portugal.
Europeans wanted spices and gold, but had little to sell.
One ship from a fleet of five sailed round the world.
Portuguese ships with cannon took control of several Asian ports.
In 1519, Spanish soldiers arrived in Mexico and fought a great king.
In 1532, a Spanish captain captured a powerful ruler in Peru.
Diseases from Europe killed millions of people in the Americas.
When many people were sick, nobody could grow food.
Nobody knows exactly how many people died, but it was very many.
With so many people gone, Europeans took over their land.
Spain took great amounts of silver from mines in the Americas.
Plants and animals crossed the ocean in both directions.
The potato grew well in cool Europe and fed many people.
American crops also helped feed more people in Africa and China.
Europe gained greatly, but the peoples of the Americas lost much.
Many native peoples survived, and their children live today.
Europeans wanted sugar, and they grew it on big farms.
Farm owners bought enslaved Africans to do the hard work.
Millions of Africans were forced onto ships and taken away.
The voyage lasted weeks, and many people died on the way.
Enslaved people worked from sunrise to sunset without pay.
Cotton, tobacco and coffee were also grown by enslaved workers.
Trade in sugar and cotton made some merchants and ports rich.
The slave trade hurt many families and towns in Africa.
In 1791, enslaved people in Haiti rose up and fought for freedom.
Slowly, many countries made slavery against the law.
Britain had plenty of coal, and much of it was near the surface.
Wood became rare, so people started to burn coal instead.
Deep mines filled with water, and pumping it out was hard.
In 1712, Thomas Newcomen built an engine that used steam.
James Watt improved the engine so that it used less coal.
Light cotton cloth from India was very popular in Europe.
New machines could spin many threads at one time.
Big machines in factories made cotton cloth very cheaply.
Factory work was hard, long and sometimes very dangerous.
Experts still argue about why this change started in Britain.
Fair rules help people trust each other and start businesses.
Where kings took what they wanted, people hid their money.
In England, a war between the king and Parliament took place.
In 1688, Parliament gained real power over the king.
Britain could borrow money cheaply because it paid its debts.
These new rules did not help everyone in the same way.
Laws protected inventors, so they could earn money from their ideas.
Many people could share the risk of a big voyage.
The Dutch were rich traders, and Amsterdam was a busy port.
Spain had lots of silver, but it still ran short of money.
In 1825, the first public steam railway opened in England.
Trains moved goods much faster and cheaper than horses.
Wires sent news fast, and big ships with engines crossed the oceans.
Other countries wanted to copy the new British machines.
Belgium was the first country in Europe to copy Britain.
Germany and the United States built many new factories too.
Schools taught more people to read, to count and to think.
Steel and electric power changed industry again in new ways.
Late starters could copy what already worked well.
Switzerland had no coal or sea, but it still grew rich.
Two hundred years ago, most people were poor and lives were short.
In 1796, a doctor found a way to protect people from smallpox.
A doctor in London showed that dirty water could spread disease.
Cities built sewers and pipes for clean water.
Healthy people can work, learn and earn more money.
People today live more than twice as long as in 1800.

When more children lived, families had fewer babies.
For many centuries, people's incomes hardly grew at all.
Today the gap between rich and poor countries is very wide.

Japan built schools, railways, banks and factories very quickly.
Japan became strong, but it also fought wars and took colonies.
After 1950, four East Asian economies grew very fast.
In Korea and Taiwan, many small farmers got their own land.
Singapore is a tiny island, but it became very rich.
After 1978, China allowed more people to start businesses.
India also began to grow fast after changes in the 1990s.
Some countries in Africa have grown very fast too.

In parts of Africa, flies made it hard to keep cattle.
European powers divided up Africa, and they drew lines on maps.
Colonies sent raw materials to Europe, and gained little in return.

B1B2: Look at the world today and you will see a huge gap. People in some countries live long, comfortable lives, while people in others still struggle to pay for food and medicine.
A baby born in one country may live decades longer than a baby born in another. Medicine, schools and food all depend a great deal on how rich a country is.
Economists call a country rich when the average person earns and produces a great deal. Money is not everything, but it usually buys better food, safer homes and more years of schooling.

The gap between rich and poor countries has not always looked the way it does now. About a thousand years ago, some of the world's most advanced cities stood in China, India and the Middle East, not in Europe.
Baghdad, in the Middle East, was a centre of learning, with libraries, translators and astronomers. Cairo, in Egypt, and Kaifeng, in China, were also among the largest and busiest cities on Earth.
In the year 1000, most people in northern Europe lived in small villages and worked the land. Their towns were small, their roads were poor, and few of them could read.
That is the puzzle at the heart of this book. How did a few countries in the far west of Eurasia end up so much richer than the great cities of the East?
Historians have offered three main kinds of answer to the puzzle. Some point to place, such as climate, crops and coasts; some to rules, such as laws and governments; and some to plain chance.
One thing must be made clear from the very start. No group of people is born cleverer than another, and any answer that says so is wrong.
To understand the past, experts dig up old tools, read old records and study old numbers. Where the evidence is thin or experts disagree, this book will say so.
For most of human history, people lived in small groups of hunters and gatherers. They moved with the seasons and took their food from the wild.
Fire let people cook, keep warm and scare away wild animals. With tools of stone, bone and wood they could hunt, cut meat and sew clothes.
Modern humans first lived in Africa, then spread slowly to Asia, Europe and Australia. They reached the Americas at least fifteen thousand years ago.
In caves in France and Spain, people painted horses, bison and hands on the walls. Their art, music and language show minds just as clever as ours.
Hunting bands knew every plant and animal in their land. They owned little that they could not carry, and in most groups people shared food.
During the last ice age, great sheets of ice covered much of the north. The climate was cold, dry and changeable, so growing crops would have been very hard.
About twelve thousand years ago the ice age ended, and the world grew warmer and wetter. The seas rose, and in time Britain became an island of its own.
In the Levant, in western Asia, some hunters settled in villages about fourteen thousand years ago. They lived there all year round, and this was long before anyone farmed.
They cut wild wheat and barley with sharp stone blades and ground the seeds on flat stones. Seeds were stored in pits for the hungry months.
Nobody sat down one day and decided to invent farming. It happened slowly, over hundreds of years, and historians still argue about why it began.
The Fertile Crescent is an arc of land in western Asia. Wild wheat, barley, peas and lentils grew there, and all of them were easy to farm.
Each year, farmers kept the biggest and best seeds to plant again. Over many generations the plants changed, until they could hardly grow without human help.
In China, people began to grow rice beside the Yangtze river in the south. In the drier north, along the Yellow River, they grew millet.
In Mexico, farmers slowly turned a wild grass called teosinte into maize, which Americans also call corn. Its early cobs were tiny, and the change took thousands of years.
High in the Andes, in South America, farmers grew potatoes and a grain called quinoa. They also raised llamas, which gave them wool and carried loads.
Africa had its own crops too, and it did not copy them from anywhere. South of the Sahara, people grew sorghum, millet, African rice and yams, all plants that they found in their own lands.
In the highlands of New Guinea, people drained wet ground and planted taro, bananas and sugar cane. Archaeologists have found traces of these gardens that are thousands of years old.
Altogether, farming began independently in several parts of the world, and in each place with different plants. Eastern North America, for example, had its own crops, such as sunflowers.

Early farming was hard labour, and some skeletons suggest that early farmers were shorter and less healthy than hunters. Even so, a field could feed far more people than the same land could as hunting ground.
From each home region, farming spread outward very slowly. It reached Europe about eight thousand years ago, and Britain a few thousand years after that.
Farming produced much more food from the same land. People settled in villages, built houses and had more children who lived.
Unlike meat, grain could be stored for years, which meant it could be owned and counted. Some families grew richer than others, and rulers soon learned to take a share.
There are hundreds of thousands of kinds of wild plant, but very few make good crops. Wheat, rice and maize alone provide a very large share of the food that people eat.
Wild wheat and barley have large seeds, grow quickly and give a good harvest in a single season. Oak trees take years to bear nuts, and acorns are bitter and need much work.
Some regions simply had more useful wild plants and animals than others. The Fertile Crescent was lucky in this way, and its farmers got a head start of thousands of years.
Asia and Europe stretch a long way from east to west. Places at the same distance from the equator have similar climates, so crops like wheat could spread easily across them.
The Americas and Africa stretch mostly from north to south, and they cross deserts, jungles and high mountains. Maize took thousands of years to travel north from Mexico to eastern North America.
Australia had few plants that suited farming, and its peoples did not farm. They managed the land with fire and built fish traps, and they kept one of the oldest living cultures.
More people meant more thinkers, makers and traders for the world. A big population can support specialists, and an idea in one place can be improved by someone in another.
Yet a head start is not a promise of a lasting lead. The lands where farming began, such as Iraq and Syria, are not among the richest today, so something more than farming must matter.
In western Asia, people began to tame wild animals about ten thousand years ago. Their first farm animals were sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.
Out of all the large wild animals, only a few could be tamed. A farm animal must stay calm, breed well in captivity and eat food that people can find.
Big animals such as oxen could pull a plough through heavy soil. One farmer could now work much more land, and carts could carry heavy goods to market.
Farm animals gave much more than meat to the people who kept them. People used their milk and made cheese, spun their wool into cloth, and made leather from their skins.
Horses were tamed on the grasslands of central Asia about five thousand years ago. Camels were tamed in Arabia, and they could cross deserts that no ox could.
The Americas had few animals that could be tamed. The llama could carry light loads, but it was too small to pull a plough or a heavy cart.
Archaeologists have found small toys with wheels in ancient Mexico. Without large animals to pull carts, the wheel was never put to heavy work.
Living close to animals let germs jump to humans. Flu, measles and smallpox are all thought to have started in animals, and they spread easily in crowded villages.
Farming peoples suffered terrible epidemics, but over many generations they built up some resistance. A child who survived measles, for example, was usually protected for life.
Peoples who lived far away had never met these germs and had no protection. This would matter terribly, and we will return to it later in the story.
When farmers grew more food than they needed, some people no longer had to farm. They became potters, builders, priests, soldiers and scribes, and towns began to grow.
Mesopotamia means the land between the two great rivers. Between the Tigris and the Euphrates the rain was scarce, so farmers dug canals to carry river water to their fields.
More than five thousand years ago, Uruk became one of the first great cities. Tens of thousands of people may have lived there, behind high mud-brick walls.
In a city like Uruk, the temple was more than a place to pray. It stored grain, gave out food and wages, and kept careful records of who owned what.
City workshops made pots on spinning wheels, wove cloth and shaped metal. Traders weighed silver and carried these goods to towns far away.
In Egypt, the river Nile flooded every year and left rich soil for farming. About forty-five centuries ago, its kings built huge pyramids with the help of thousands of workers.
In the Indus Valley, in what is now Pakistan and India, people built cities with straight streets and covered drains. Mohenjo-daro was one of the biggest of these early cities.
Cities also grew up on the Yellow River in China, and in Peru and Mexico, with no contact with the Old World. Caral, in Peru, is about five thousand years old.
Cities were also very unequal places for people to live in. Rulers and priests lived in fine houses, while most people farmed, carried loads or dug canals for little reward.
A big city needed rules, records and someone in charge. These needs led, step by step, to writing, to laws and to the first governments.
Writing did not begin with poems or with any stories. About five thousand years ago in Mesopotamia, clerks first used marks on clay to count grain, beer and sheep.
Scribes pressed a cut reed into wet clay to make wedge-shaped marks, called cuneiform. Learning to write took years at school, and only a few people were trained.
Egypt, China and Mexico each developed writing on their own. Egyptian scribes used picture signs called hieroglyphs, and Chinese writers carved questions on animal bones.
Writing made laws, contracts and letters possible for the first time. It also let stories and knowledge travel to people far away, and survive long after their authors had died.
Rulers took a share of the harvest as tax. They used it to pay officials, build temples and canals, and feed soldiers.
About 3,750 years ago, King Hammurabi of Babylon had a long list of laws carved on a tall stone. Anyone who could read, or who had a reader, could learn the rules.
A state with plenty of food and tax money could pay for a large army. Some rulers used armies to conquer their neighbours and to build the first empires.
A large empire needed officials, roads and fast messengers. The Persian Empire, about 2,500 years ago, ruled many lands and used a long royal road with relay stations.
The Inca Empire in the Andes had no writing like ours. Its officials kept accounts and records with bundles of knotted cords called khipu.
States could keep order and build useful things such as canals and walls. They also demanded taxes, forced labour and soldiers, and ordinary people paid the price.
People learned to mix copper with tin to make bronze about five thousand years ago. Bronze was harder than copper, so it made better tools and weapons.
Tin is rare, and it is found in only a few places. Traders carried it hundreds of miles to the cities where bronze was made, which linked far-off lands.
Iron ore is common, and it can be found almost everywhere. When people learned to work it, about 3,200 years ago, even ordinary farmers could afford strong iron tools.
Chinese ironworkers learned to melt iron and pour it into moulds about 2,500 years ago. Europe did not do this on a large scale until many centuries later.
The first coins appeared in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, about 2,600 years ago. A stamped coin was easy to carry, and everyone could agree on its value.
From about 2,100 years ago, caravans of camels carried silk, spices and silver along the Silk Roads. These routes joined China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean.
Along these roads, wheat travelled east and millet and rice moved west and south. Indian mathematicians invented the number zero, and the idea later reached Europe through Arab scholars.
People in China were making paper about two thousand years ago. It was cheaper than silk or animal skin, and it slowly spread west along the trade routes.
Merchants, monks and travellers carried religions and stories as well as goods. Buddhism, for example, travelled from India to China along the Silk Roads.
Trade brought great wealth, but it also carried real risk. Diseases travelled along the same roads as goods, and great epidemics sometimes followed the merchants.
A single ship could carry as much as hundreds of carts, and it did not need a road. So peoples who lived on coasts and rivers could trade more cheaply.
The Mediterranean Sea lies between Europe, Africa and Asia, and it acted like a great highway. Phoenician and Greek sailors traded and built colonies along its shores.
At its height the Roman Empire controlled the whole Mediterranean coast. Its roads and ships carried grain from Egypt to feed the great city of Rome.
The western Roman Empire fell in the year 476, after a long decline. Roads decayed, trade shrank, and many cities in western Europe became much smaller than they had been before.
In the Indian Ocean, the monsoon winds blow one way in summer and the other way in winter. Sailors used them to travel between East Africa, Arabia, India and China.
Along the coast of East Africa, Swahili cities such as Kilwa grew rich. They sold gold and ivory from the inland and bought cloth and porcelain from Asia.
Under the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago, China built large ships with many masts. Sailors used the compass, and merchants used paper money to settle their accounts.
Camels crossed the Sahara carrying salt from the north and gold from West Africa. The empire of Mali grew rich from this trade, and its ruler Mansa Musa became famous across the world.

Polynesian sailors crossed thousands of miles of the Pacific Ocean in double canoes. They steered by the stars, the waves and the flight of birds, and they settled the islands from Hawaii to New Zealand.
By about the year 1000, a great web of trade joined Asia, Africa and Europe. The richest centres were in the Middle East, India and China, and western Europe lay at the far edge.
Gunpowder, the magnetic compass and printing were all first used in China. Europeans later copied these inventions and improved them for their own uses.
In Germany, about 1450, Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with movable metal letters. Books became much cheaper, and they spread across Europe within a few decades.
Europe was not one empire but a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies and free cities. Mountains, rivers and seas made it hard for any single ruler to conquer everything.
Rival kings needed money, soldiers and skilled people, and they competed for them. An idea that one ruler rejected might be welcomed by another, so it could survive.
In 1521 the German preacher Martin Luther was declared an outlaw. A local prince hid him, and printing presses carried his ideas across Europe.
Christopher Columbus asked several rulers to pay for a voyage west to Asia. Most refused, but because Europe had many courts, he could keep trying until Spain agreed.
Between 1405 and 1433 China sent enormous treasure fleets under Admiral Zheng He as far as East Africa. Then the Ming court stopped the voyages and let the great ships rot.
A single government can keep the peace over a huge area and build great works. But it can also stop a good idea with one decision, as it did with the voyages of Zheng He.
In Italy, cities like Venice, Genoa and Florence grew rich from trade with the East. Their bankers made loans, and their merchants used careful bookkeeping to track their money.
In the twelfth century, scholars in places like Toledo in Spain translated Arabic books into Latin. Europe was a student of the wider world before it became a teacher.
Portugal lies on the Atlantic edge of Europe, far from Asia. In the 1400s its sailors explored the coast of Africa a little further south each year, looking for gold and a way to Asia.
The Portuguese built a light ship called the caravel, which could sail well against the wind. Sailors also used the compass and a tool called the astrolabe to find their position.
In 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa. His crew turned back, but they had shown that a sea route to the Indian Ocean might exist.
In 1492 Christopher Columbus left Spain with three small ships and sailed west. After about ten weeks at sea, he reached islands in the Caribbean on 12 October.
In 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached Calicut, on the coast of India. He had completed the route to the spice markets that Portugal had hoped for.
Europeans wanted spices, silk and gold, but Asian markets had little interest in the goods that Europe produced. They mostly paid for what they bought with silver and gold.
In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan sailed from Spain with five ships. He was killed in the Philippines in 1521, but one ship returned in 1522, the first to go all the way around the world.
Portuguese ships carried heavy cannon, and they used them to seize ports such as Goa and Malacca. They controlled many harbours, but they did not conquer the great empires of Asia.
In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico with about five hundred soldiers. With thousands of local allies who resented Aztec rule, and with the help of disease, he overthrew the Aztec Empire in 1521.
In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa with a small force. The Inca Empire had just suffered a civil war and a wave of disease, and this made it much easier to defeat.
When Europeans arrived, they brought smallpox, measles and flu. The peoples of the Americas had never met these diseases, and millions of them died.
When a disease struck, whole families fell ill at once. With no one strong enough to nurse the sick or tend the fields, hunger followed, and more people died.
Historians cannot be certain how many people died, because no one counted. Many believe that the population of the Americas fell by the majority within about a hundred years.
With so many people gone, kingdoms collapsed and fields were left empty. Europeans took the land, and later millions of settlers arrived to farm it.
After 1545 the huge silver mine at Potosi, in the Andes, poured silver into Spain's treasury. Much of it was forced out of local workers, and then it spread into world trade.
After 1492 plants and animals crossed the Atlantic in both directions. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chillies went east, while wheat, sugar, cattle and horses went west.
The potato grew well in the cool, wet climate of northern Europe. It gave more food per field than most grains, and the population of Europe rose.
American crops spread to Asia and Africa as well. Maize and cassava became important in Africa, and sweet potatoes and maize helped feed more people in China.
Europe gained land, silver and new crops from the Americas. The Indigenous peoples of the Americas paid for those gains with their lives, their land and much of their freedom.
The native peoples of the Americas did not disappear. Millions of their descendants live today, and they still speak languages such as Quechua and Maya and keep their traditions alive.
Europeans loved sugar, and it sold for high prices. Planters in Brazil and the Caribbean set up huge farms called plantations to grow it, and they needed many workers.
Many native workers had died, and European servants were too few. So planters turned to the trade in enslaved Africans, which merchants and rulers on both sides of the Atlantic organised.
Over about three hundred and fifty years, more than twelve million Africans were forced onto ships and carried across the Atlantic. Many people did not survive the long and terrible voyage.
The journey across the Atlantic, called the Middle Passage, lasted weeks. People were chained, packed close together and given little food or water, and many fell ill and died.
On plantations, enslaved men, women and children worked from dawn to dark without pay. The law treated them as property, and families could be separated and sold.

Sugar was not the only crop that was grown this way. Tobacco, rice, coffee and, later, cotton were also grown by enslaved workers, and by 1860 almost four million people were enslaved in the United States alone.
Ports such as Bristol, Liverpool, Lisbon and Nantes grew rich from the trade. Historians still debate how much slavery added to Europe's economic growth overall.
The slave trade took millions of people from Africa, and it caused wars to capture more. Some kingdoms grew strong by selling captives, but many communities lost their young and strong.

In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, and in 1804 their country became independent as Haiti. Later France demanded a huge payment from Haiti, which held the country back.

Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and ended slavery in its colonies in 1833, but it paid compensation to the owners, not to the enslaved. Slavery ended in the United States in 1865 and in Brazil in 1888.
Britain was lucky to have large amounts of coal, and much of it lay close to the surface. Many mines were also near rivers and ports, so the coal was cheap to move.
Over the centuries, much of Britain's wood was cut down for building and fuel. As wood grew scarce and dear, people began to burn coal to heat their homes and to work metal.
As miners dug deeper, water began to flood the tunnels. Pumps worked by horses were slow and costly, so mine owners wanted a better kind of engine.
In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine to pump water out of a mine. It used a great deal of coal, but at a coal mine, coal was cheap.
In the 1760s James Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, added a separate chamber to cool the steam. His engine used far less coal, and it could soon turn wheels as well as pump water.
Fine cotton cloth from India was popular in Europe, and it was cheaper and lighter than wool. British makers wanted to copy it, and they found ways to make it with machines.
In the 1760s and 1770s inventors built the spinning jenny, the water frame and later the mule. With them, one worker could spin dozens of threads at the same time.
Machines were grouped together in large mills powered by water and later by steam. The cloth they made was cheap, but the raw cotton came mostly from enslaved workers in the Americas.
Factory work was long, loud and dangerous, and children worked there as well as adults. Laws such as the Factory Act of 1833 began to protect children, but real improvement came slowly.
Historians still argue about why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain. Some stress coal and high wages, others empire and trade, and others science, law and government.
People will only build a business or plant an orchard if they believe they can keep the profit. Fair courts, honest contracts and protected property give them that confidence.
Where a ruler could seize property, or refuse to repay a loan, people hid their wealth. They did not invest it, and the whole country was poorer.
In the 1640s, England fought a civil war between the king and Parliament. In 1649 Parliament had King Charles I put to death, and it was a shock to all of Europe.
In 1688 Parliament invited a new king and queen, William and Mary, to take the throne. The Bill of Rights of 1689 said that the king could not make laws or raise taxes without Parliament.
Because Parliament controlled taxes and promised to repay debts, lenders trusted the government. The Bank of England began in 1694, and Britain could borrow cheaply to build ships and fight wars.
These rules did not benefit everyone in the same way. Only a small group of men could vote, and the poor often lost access to common fields when landowners fenced them off.
In Britain a law from 1624 let inventors hold a patent, which gave them sole rights to their idea for a number of years. This rewarded inventors and encouraged them to publish their designs.
Joint-stock companies let many investors share the cost and the risk of a voyage, and insurance paid out if a ship was lost. Some of these companies, however, used armies and force.

The Dutch Republic became one of the richest countries in the 1600s. Amsterdam had banks, a stock exchange and a tradition of welcoming people of different faiths, and its merchants sailed all over the world.
Spain received huge amounts of silver from the Americas, yet it went bankrupt several times. Wealth alone was not enough, and rules, as we have seen, can change.
In 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in northern England. George Stephenson's locomotive pulled coal wagons and passengers along iron rails.
Railways cut the cost and the time of moving goods very sharply. A farmer could now sell his milk or his wheat in a city far away, and town markets joined into one large market.
The telegraph carried news in minutes instead of days, and steamships crossed the ocean on a regular timetable. A cable under the Atlantic joined America and Europe in 1866.

Other countries wanted British machines, and Britain tried to stop engineers and drawings from leaving, but it failed. Samuel Slater, for example, memorised the plans and built a cotton mill in America.
Belgium was the first country on the European continent to industrialise. It had coal and iron close together, an English-trained engineer called John Cockerill, and a government that built railways.
Germany and the United States soon built factories of their own. Germany joined its small states into a customs union in 1834, and both countries built railways across wide lands.
Countries that built schools had more people who could read, count and learn new skills. Prussia, in Germany, made schooling compulsory early, and its universities led in science.
From the middle of the 1800s, cheap steel, electricity and new chemicals began a second wave of industry. Germany and the United States led it, and Britain's lead began to fade.
A country that starts late can copy the machines that already work and avoid early mistakes. But it needs skilled workers, schools and stable rules to do so, and many countries lacked them.
Switzerland has mountains, no coast and no coal, yet it became one of the richest countries. It used water power, trained its workers well, and became famous for watches, machines and banking.
Two hundred years ago nearly everyone was poor, and lives were short. In much of the world about one child in three died before the age of five.
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox seemed safe from smallpox. He tested the idea on a boy, and vaccination was born.
In 1854 cholera struck a part of London, and the doctor John Snow marked the deaths on a map. He traced them to one water pump, which showed that dirty water was spreading the disease.
In the 1860s the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a huge system of sewers in London. Cities around the world later laid pipes for clean water, and deaths from disease fell.
Healthy children go to school more often, and healthy adults can work for more years. Better health therefore helped to make countries richer, and richer countries could afford better health.

The average person on Earth in 1800 lived only about thirty years, partly because so many children died. Today the world average is more than seventy, though it is much lower in the poorest countries.
Around 1800 only about one adult in eight in the world could read. Governments, churches and families slowly built schools, and today about nine adults in ten can read.
When children stopped dying so often, families began to have fewer babies. They could spend more on each child's health and school, and the gains grew from one generation to the next.
For thousands of years the average person's income hardly changed. After about 1800 it began to climb in a few countries, and economists call the widening gap the Great Divergence.
In 1800 the richest country was perhaps three or four times richer than the poorest. Today the gap is far wider, with the richest countries dozens of times richer than the poorest.
In 1868 Japan's leaders began the Meiji period, and they decided to learn from the West. Japan sent officials abroad to study, and it never became a colony.
Japan made primary school compulsory in 1872, and the first railway opened the same year. The government also built factories, set up banks and hired foreign experts to teach local workers.
Japan's success also had a very dark side for others. It built a strong army and navy, took Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910, and later fought a terrible war, which brought suffering to many people.
After the 1950s four East Asian economies grew very fast. South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong built their wealth by selling goods abroad and by teaching their people well.
Before they industrialised, South Korea and Taiwan carried out land reforms. They broke up large estates and gave land to farmers, who then worked harder and saved more.

Singapore is a small island with almost no natural resources. After it became independent in 1965 it built a busy port, kept its courts honest and taught its children in English and in local languages.
After 1978 China's government began to let farmers sell extra crops and to let companies trade with other countries. Hundreds of millions of people escaped extreme poverty in the years that followed.

India started to open up its economy in 1991, and since then it has grown fast, especially in software and services. It grew fast, especially in software and services, though many millions of Indians still live in poverty.

Some African countries have also grown very fast in recent years. Botswana used its diamond earnings well, with honest courts and good rules, and the island of Mauritius moved from sugar to clothes and tourism.
There is no single recipe that works in every country. Even so, countries that caught up usually had good schools, good health, trade with the world, a period of peace and a government that worked.
A country with no coast must send its goods through the ports of its neighbours. That raises costs and slows trade, although Switzerland and Austria show that it can be overcome.
Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes, and it still kills hundreds of thousands of people each year, mostly young children in Africa. It also weakens workers and keeps children out of school.
In parts of Africa, tsetse flies carry a disease that kills cattle and horses. This made it hard to keep animals for ploughing, carrying loads and fertilising the soil.
In 1884 and 1885 European powers met in Berlin and made rules for dividing Africa. They drew borders on maps with little thought for the people who lived there, and no African leader was invited.
Colonial rulers often built railways from mines and plantations straight to the ports. The raw materials were shipped abroad, and few schools or factories were built for local people.
India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, and Ghana followed in 1957. In 1960 alone, seventeen African countries became free, but many of them had few trained officials or engineers.
War damages roads, schools and farms, and it destroys trust between people. A country in the middle of a civil war can lose many years of growth, and sometimes it never fully recovers.
Oil and diamonds can bring huge sums of money, but rulers who get this easy money may not need to tax their people. Norway and Botswana, however, have used theirs well for everyone.

Many poor countries borrowed money and then struggled to pay it back. The prices of crops like coffee also go up and down, and rich countries sometimes protect their own farmers with taxes on imports.
Poor countries can sometimes leap ahead in new ways. In Kenya a mobile-phone money service, started in 2007, let people send money without a bank, and it spread across the country.
In 1347 trading ships brought the plague, known as the Black Death, to Europe from the Black Sea. Within a few years it had spread to nearly every country on the continent.
After the plague there were far fewer workers, so those who survived could ask for higher wages. In western Europe, the old ties that bound peasants to their lords began to weaken.

Storms, sudden deaths and lucky meetings have all changed history. When a storm helped to scatter the Spanish Armada in 1588, England was saved from invasion, but nobody can say what would have followed otherwise.
War destroys homes, factories and the trust between people. After 1945 Germany and Japan lay in ruins, yet within a few decades they were among the richest countries in the world.
No people is naturally cleverer than any other people on Earth. A baby born anywhere can learn to do anything, and the differences in wealth come from circumstances.
Economists broadly agree that peace, good health, good schools, honest courts and trade all help a country to grow. They still argue about how much each matters and which should come first.
Place gave some peoples a head start, such as good crops and good coasts. Rules decided how well that start was used, and chance added its own surprises.
We cannot rerun history to test our ideas, so every neat explanation deserves some caution. The honest answer is that many causes worked together, and some of them are still unknown.
Over the centuries the richest places have changed many times. Cities in Mesopotamia, then China, Italy and the Netherlands, then Britain and the United States have each been among the richest.
The list of rich countries has changed many times, and it will change again. A poor country today may be a rich one in a few generations, if the conditions are right.
C1C2: If you could look down at the Earth at night, you would see a strange pattern: some lands blaze with electric light, while others lie almost dark. Behind that pattern are very different lives, in which one person may expect comfort, good health and a long old age, and another a daily struggle to survive. This book asks the oldest question in economics, which is why the world ended up so uneven.

Where a child happens to be born is one of the biggest facts about the life that child will lead. In the richest countries a baby can expect to reach old age, while in the poorest the difference in life expectancy can be measured in decades. That gap is not a small one, and it is the reason the question in this book matters.

When economists call a country rich, they usually mean that the average person there produces and earns a great deal in a year. Wealth is a blunt measure of a good life, and it hides large differences between families, yet it tends to travel with longer lives, better schools and cleaner water. That is why historians treat it as a useful, if imperfect, place to start.

The present order of rich and poor is not ancient, and it is certainly not permanent. A thousand years ago the busiest markets, the finest silks and the most skilled craftsmen were found in Asia far more often than in the villages of northern Europe. Anyone who had tried to predict then which region would grow richest would very probably have guessed wrong.

Baghdad, on the river Tigris, gathered scholars who translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and then added discoveries of their own. Cairo, in Egypt, and Kaifeng, in China, were also among the largest and busiest cities anywhere, full of shops, workshops and wharves. For a traveller of that age, northern Europe would have looked like the quiet edge of the map.

Around the year 1000, most people in northern Europe were farmers who lived in small villages of timber and thatch, close to the soil and to hunger. Towns were modest, roads were poor, and only a small number of monks and nobles could read. Nothing in that picture suggested that this corner of the world would soon change the global balance of power.

That strange reversal is the puzzle at the very heart of this whole book about wealth. How did a handful of countries on the western fringe of Eurasia come to overtake the great civilisations of the East, and why did the lead last so long? It is a question that every curious person has asked, and the honest answer is longer, and stranger, than a single cause.

Over the years scholars have offered three broad kinds of explanation, and each deserves a fair hearing. Some look to place, meaning the climate, the plants, the animals and the coasts that nature happened to provide. Others look to rules, meaning the laws and governments that people built, and a third group looks to chance, meaning the wars, plagues and accidents that nobody planned.

One point has to be made clearly before the story of the world's wealth can begin. There is no evidence that any people is naturally cleverer, harder-working or more inventive than another, and any theory that quietly depends on such a claim should be thrown away. The differences in this book come from circumstances, which means from geography, history and the choices of those who held power.

The story that follows has been pieced together by archaeologists digging up old tools, historians reading old records, and economists studying numbers that stretch back centuries. Some of it is well established, and some is still argued over with great energy, and where that is so the book will say so plainly. We begin at the very beginning, with the people who had not yet planted a single seed.

For almost all of the time that humans have existed, our ancestors lived in small bands that hunted animals and gathered wild plants. They followed the seasons across the land, camping where food was plentiful and moving on when it ran short.
