By comparison, farming, cities, writing and money are all very recent inventions, no more than a few thousand years old.

Fire was one of the great tools of early humans, for it cooked their food, warmed their nights and kept hungry predators at a distance. With skilfully shaped stone, bone and wood they made spears, scrapers and needles, and sewed the clothes that carried them into freezing lands. Such knowledge was passed down by talking and showing, from one generation to the next.

Our species began in Africa, and over tens of thousands of years its members spread into Asia, Europe and Australia, adapting to deserts, forests and frozen plains. People had reached the Americas by at least fifteen thousand years ago, though scholars still argue about exactly when and by which routes. It was one of the greatest journeys in history, and it was made on foot and in small boats.

In caves in France and Spain, artists working by torchlight painted horses, bison and lions with astonishing skill tens of thousands of years ago. Bone flutes and carved figures survive as well, along with the traces of languages that must have been as rich as our own. These people were fully modern in mind, which is worth remembering whenever we compare societies of later times.

A hunting band knew its territory in astonishing detail, from the berries that ripened in each season to the paths that every herd would take. Because the group had to keep moving, it owned little beyond what it could carry, and in most such societies food was shared. Large differences in wealth between families were therefore unusual, since there was little to store and little to hand down.

During the last ice age, huge sheets of ice lay over much of northern Europe, Asia and North America, and the air everywhere was colder and drier than it is today. The climate also swung unpredictably, which would have defeated anyone trying to plant crops and wait for the harvest. Hunting and gathering was the safer way to live, and it remained so for a very long time.

About twelve thousand years ago the ice age ended, and the climate settled into a warmer, wetter and far steadier pattern that has lasted ever since. As the ice melted, the seas rose and drowned low coasts, and a land bridge disappeared beneath the waves so that Britain became an island. Plants spread, animals multiplied, and for the first time the climate favoured people willing to try growing food.

In the Levant, the lands at the eastern end of the Mediterranean, some peoples settled in villages as early as fourteen thousand years ago. They had found that wild grains and game were so plentiful there that they no longer needed to wander, and so they built houses of stone. Settling down, remarkably enough, came before the first farming rather than coming after it, which surprises many people.

These early villagers cut wild wheat and barley with sickles set with razor-sharp stone blades, then pounded the seeds on grinding stones to make flour. They stored surplus grain in pits so that they would have something to eat in the hungry months. Without knowing it, they had taken the first step toward the idea of planting.

No one woke up one morning and decided to invent farming, for the change crept forward over hundreds of generations and began in different places at different times. Historians still debate what pushed people to start, whether it was a changing climate, a growing population, or simply curiosity. What we can say is that once it began, almost everything else in this book followed from it.

The Fertile Crescent is an arc of land that curves from the eastern Mediterranean through what is now Iraq. Wild wheat, barley, peas and lentils grew there in abundance, and each of them turned out to be unusually easy to cultivate. Farming began in this region about eleven thousand years ago, and it was among the earliest places on Earth where it did.

Each year farmers saved the largest seeds from the plants that were easiest to harvest, and planted them in the next spring. Over many generations the crops changed in ways that no one intended, growing bigger seeds and holding on to them instead of scattering them. By the end of the process the plants depended on people almost as much as people depended on them.

In China, farming grew up in two distinct regions, with rice cultivated in the warm, wet south along the Yangtze river and millet in the cooler, drier north beside the Yellow River. Both were domesticated roughly nine thousand years ago, and each region built its own farming traditions. The rice paddy, flooded and carefully tended, would later feed a large share of humanity.

In what is now Mexico, farmers began working on a modest wild grass called teosinte, whose seed heads held only a few small kernels. Through many centuries of patient selection it became maize, a plant so changed that it can no longer scatter its own seed. Grown beside beans and squash, it formed a trio of crops that fed whole civilisations of the Americas.

High in the Andes mountains of South America, farmers learned to grow potatoes in thin air and cold soil, together with a nutritious grain called quinoa. They also kept llamas, which gave wool and could carry light loads along narrow mountain paths. Such crops would one day cross the oceans and change the diet of countries on the far side of the world.

Africa had its own farming revolutions, quite separate from those in Asia, for the crops that were domesticated south of the Sahara were plants that grew in the region itself. Sorghum and millet suited the dry grasslands, African rice grew in river floodplains, and yams thrived in the forests of the west. Farmers there worked with what their own land offered, just as farmers elsewhere did.

In the misty highlands of New Guinea, people dug drainage ditches through swampy ground and planted taro, bananas and sugar cane. Archaeologists have uncovered the traces of these ancient gardens, which show that farming there is thousands of years old and probably began on its own. It is a reminder that early agriculture was not a single invention but many.

Taken together, these cases show that farming was invented independently in several parts of the world, each time with different plants and each time without help from outsiders. Eastern North America, for instance, produced its own crops, among them sunflowers and a species of squash. Whenever people had suitable plants and a steady climate, it seems, some of them began to farm.

Early farming was heavy, repetitive work, and evidence from ancient skeletons suggests that in some places the first farmers were shorter and sicker than the hunters before them. Yet a single field could feed many times more people than the same land could as a hunting ground, so populations grew regardless. Once there were more mouths to feed, it was almost impossible to go back.

From each of its homelands, farming spread outward at a walking pace, carried partly by farmers who moved to new land and partly by neighbours who copied what they saw. It reached southern Europe about eight thousand years ago, and Britain a couple of thousand years later. Wherever it landed, it changed how people lived, how many of them there were, and who they could become.

Farming produced far more food from each patch of land than hunting and gathering could, and that changed everything around it. People built permanent villages of mud and timber, stored grain in jars, and raised larger families, since a settled mother could care for more young children at once. Populations that had once been counted in dozens began, over the centuries, to be counted in hundreds and then thousands.

Unlike a fresh kill, a harvest of grain could be stored for months or years, and anything that can be stored can be owned, counted, traded and guarded. Some families grew richer than their neighbours, and powerful people discovered that they could take a share of the stores for themselves. Rank, property and inequality between families were largely products of the farming world, and they have shaped human societies ever since.

Of the hundreds of thousands of wild plant species on Earth, only a few hundred were ever successfully farmed, and a small handful feed most of humanity. Wheat, rice and maize alone supply a very large share of the calories that people eat today. The lands that happened to have such plants growing wild were given a remarkable head start.

Wild wheat and barley had everything that an early farmer wanted: large seeds, quick growth and a harvest within a single season. Oaks were a very different case, for they take years to bear fruit and their acorns are bitter and must be soaked before anyone can eat them. Many peoples valued acorns, but the tree never became a farm crop in the way that grain did.

Some regions of the world were simply better stocked than others with the wild plants and animals that could be tamed. The Fertile Crescent was fortunate in this respect, since it had cereals, pulses and several large animals within a short walk of one another, and its farmers gained a lead of thousands of years. Nobody earned that luck, and nobody deserved any less in the places where nature happened to give less.

Europe and Asia together form a vast landmass that stretches from east to west, and places at the same distance from the equator share a similar climate and day length. Crops and animals that thrived in one place could therefore be carried a very long way before they met conditions that defeated them. Some scholars find this argument persuasive, although others think it explains less than it appears to.

The Americas and Africa both run largely from north to south, so a crop travelling any distance meets deserts, mountains, rainforests and sharp changes in climate. Maize needed thousands of years to move from Mexico to the eastern part of North America, and farming in southern Africa spread slowly across the continent as farming peoples moved south. Where ideas and crops travelled slowly, the benefits of farming took far longer to reach everyone who might have used them.

Australia offered few native plants that could be turned into crops, and for tens of thousands of years its peoples did not farm. They shaped the land with careful burning, built stone traps to catch fish, and kept one of the oldest living cultures on Earth. A society without farming was not a failure, though it did not produce the surplus that supported cities.

A larger population is more than a larger number of mouths, since it also holds more potential inventors, more skilled makers and more people to trade and quarrel and compare ideas. Specialists became possible once farmers could feed others, and good ideas could be copied and improved by people far away. In this way an early advantage in food slowly turned into an advantage in knowledge.

A head start, however, is no guarantee of a lasting lead, and the evidence for that is plain. The lands where farming began, in modern Iraq and Syria, are far from the richest in the world today, so something more than early crops must be at work. Historians call this a reversal of fortune, and it will keep returning as the story unfolds.

In western Asia, people began to tame wild animals at roughly the same time as they began to sow crops, about ten thousand years ago. The first farm animals were sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, each of which had wild ancestors living in the surrounding hills. Over many generations the animals grew calmer, smaller and more useful, and they became part of the household.

Of the world's large wild mammals, only a small number were ever successfully domesticated, and the reasons are practical rather than mysterious. A farm animal must be calm enough to live among people, eat food that is easy to find, grow quickly and breed in captivity. Zebras, for example, are strong and numerous, but they are famously bad-tempered, and no one has ever made them reliable.

Once strong oxen could be harnessed to a wooden plough, a single farmer could turn over far more earth than anyone working with a hoe. The animals also provided manure to feed the soil, and later pulled carts that carried grain, stone and timber to places that could not be reached on foot. More food and easier transport together meant bigger harvests, larger markets and busier trade between one town and the next.

Animals proved to be valuable alive as well as dead, because they gave milk, from which people made yoghurt and cheese, and wool that could be spun and woven into cloth. Their skins became leather and their bones became tools, so that nothing was wasted. A flock was a store of food, clothing and wealth that walked on its own legs.

Horses were first domesticated on the grasslands of central Asia, perhaps five thousand years ago, and soon gave riders a new kind of speed in travel and in war. Camels, tamed in Arabia and North Africa, could carry heavy loads for days across deserts that would have killed an ox. These animals joined distant regions into long networks of trade and conquest, and they changed how fast news, goods and armies could travel.

The Americas, by contrast, had very few large animals that could be tamed, and many big mammals had died out at the end of the ice age. The llama could carry modest loads over mountain tracks, but it was too small and too independent to pull a plough or a heavy cart. American farmers therefore did their work by hand, and they did it superbly well.

Archaeologists have found small clay toys fitted with wheels in ancient Mexico, which proves that the idea was known. Without a large animal to pull a cart, however, wheels were not much use for hauling heavy loads over rough ground. Whether an invention matters, it turns out, depends on what else is available to go with it.

Living close to animals had a hidden cost, for germs that once infected only cattle, pigs or poultry could jump across to humans. Flu, measles and smallpox are all thought to descend from diseases of animals, and they spread easily in crowded villages where many people lived and worked in close contact. The farmyard was, in a sense, a doorway through which many new diseases entered the human world, and they stayed.

Farming peoples suffered one epidemic after another, and countless people died, yet those who survived were often left with some protection. A child who recovered from measles was usually immune for life, and over many generations the whole population became better able to resist. The result was a grim kind of inheritance, one that was paid for by the many who did not survive, and handed down to their children.

Peoples who lived in lands without such herds had never met these diseases, and their bodies had no memory of how to fight them. This was not a weakness of those peoples, only a matter of history, but it was to have terrible consequences when the world's populations finally met. We will come back to that story soon, because it changed the history of two whole continents.

Once farmers produced more grain than their own families could eat, a surplus was available to feed other people, who no longer needed to work the land. They became potters, builders, priests, soldiers and record keepers, and their skills improved because they practised one craft for a lifetime. Towns grew up around them, and over time some of those towns grew into the first real cities, with thousands of inhabitants.

Mesopotamia, a Greek name meaning the land between the rivers, lay between the Tigris and the Euphrates in what is now Iraq. Rain was scarce, so farmers dug canals to carry the river water to their fields, and the harvests were enormous. Digging and mending those canals took thousands of workers, which meant that someone had to organise them.

More than five thousand years ago the city of Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, became one of the largest settlements the world had ever seen. At its height it may have held tens of thousands of people, living behind high walls of mud brick among workshops, temples and markets. Later poets would tell of its legendary king, Gilgamesh, and make it famous for all time.

In a Mesopotamian city the temple was far more than a place of worship, for it acted as storehouse, workshop and a kind of bank. Priests collected grain from the surrounding fields, handed out rations to workers, and recorded who owed what to whom. Above the roofs rose a stepped tower called a ziggurat, which showed everyone that the gods and the rulers were close allies.

City workshops turned out pottery thrown on spinning wheels, woven cloth and metal tools, and the best of these were carried to distant towns by traders. Merchants weighed out silver on balance scales and agreed on standard measures, which let strangers trust one another's goods. The wealth of a city came from what its craftsmen could make, as well as from the harvests around it.

In Egypt the river Nile flooded every year, depositing a layer of black silt on which farmers could grow abundant crops with little effort. A strong state grew up along the river, and about forty-five centuries ago its kings, the pharaohs, ordered the building of the great pyramids. Such monuments could only be raised by a government that could feed, house and organise thousands of workers.

In the Indus Valley, in what is now Pakistan and western India, people built carefully planned cities about forty-five centuries ago. Mohenjo-daro, one of the largest, had straight streets laid out in grids, brick houses and an elaborate system of drains that many later towns lacked. The Indus people also had a script, but nobody has yet learned to read it, so much about them remains unknown.

Cities and states also emerged on their own in other parts of the world, with no contact with those in Mesopotamia. Caral, on the coast of Peru, has monumental platforms that are about five thousand years old, while the Yellow River valley of China and the lowlands of Mexico produced their own urban civilisations. Wherever farming created a large and reliable surplus, it seems that cities were never very far behind, and kings were never far behind the cities.

The first cities were, in the plainest sense, unequal societies, in which a small class of rulers and priests enjoyed fine houses, rich food and the labour of others. Most people were farmers, labourers and servants who dug canals, carried loads and handed over a share of their crops. Such inequality is one of the oldest facts in the history of wealth, and it has never entirely gone away since then.

A city of thousands needed more than farms and workshops, because someone had to settle disputes, keep records and make sure that the stores were shared and defended. Those needs gave rise, step by step, to the great inventions that follow: writing, law and the organised state. Each of them would turn out to matter greatly for the story of national wealth.

Writing did not begin with poetry, prayers or history, but with plain accounting, which may surprise many readers. About fifty-three centuries ago in Mesopotamia, temple clerks began to make marks on clay to record how much grain, beer and livestock had been received and paid out. It was simply the paperwork of a growing economy, and yet it quietly changed the whole course of human history for ever.

Scribes pressed the cut end of a reed into wet clay, leaving small wedge-shaped marks that we call cuneiform, a word meaning wedge-shaped. Mastering the hundreds of signs took years in a scribal school, where pupils copied lists on tablets under a strict teacher. Because so few people could do it, a scribe was a respected and well-placed servant of the state.

Writing was invented independently at least three more times: in Egypt, where picture signs called hieroglyphs appeared, in China, where early writers carved their questions to the gods onto animal bones, and in ancient Mexico. Each system looked quite different from the others, and none was borrowed from its neighbours. The need to keep records seems to have been so strong that people solved it again and again.

Once people could write, a king could send orders to a distant province, a merchant could sign a contract, and a teacher could leave his knowledge for pupils whom he would never meet. Stories such as the Epic of Gilgamesh were set down and survived for thousands of years, long after anyone could remember who first told them. Writing worked as a kind of memory that never tired, never forgot and never died, and that was a very powerful thing to own.

Rulers soon discovered that the most dependable source of wealth was a regular share of the harvest, collected as taxes by officials who could read and count. That grain paid for temples, canals and roads, and it also fed the soldiers who defended the city and enforced the ruler's will. Taxation was the engine of the earliest states, and it has powered governments ever since.

About 3,750 years ago, King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly three hundred laws carved on a tall pillar of black stone so that his subjects could know what was expected of them. The code dealt with trade, family, wages and crime, though its punishments were harsh and varied according to a person's rank. Even so, public rules that applied to everyone, however unevenly, were a landmark in the history of government.

A state with a full granary and a steady income from taxes could keep a standing army, and an army could take what its neighbours had. About forty-three centuries ago King Sargon of Akkad conquered the cities of southern Mesopotamia and built what is often called the first empire. Many such empires would rise and fall in the centuries that followed, each leaving its mark on the map.

To hold together a large territory, an empire needed roads, officials in every province and messengers who could cover long distances quickly. The Persian Empire, about twenty-five centuries ago, ruled lands from Egypt to the edge of India and maintained a royal road with stations where riders could change horses. Good roads helped governments to rule their lands, and they also helped merchants to carry their goods to far-off markets.

The Inca Empire, which ruled much of the Andes in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, had no written script that we know of. Instead its officials kept careful accounts of people, crops and stores using bundles of knotted cords called khipu, in which the colour and position of every knot carried meaning. It shows that a large and well-run state could be built without any writing system.

States brought real benefits, such as courts to settle disputes, canals and walls to protect the harvest, and a measure of safety from raiders. They also demanded heavy taxes, forced labour and young men for their armies, and ordinary families bore the cost. Whether rulers served their people or simply used them is a question that will return again and again in this book.

People had worked soft copper for thousands of years before they discovered that mixing it with a little tin produced bronze, a metal far harder and more durable. From about five thousand years ago, smiths poured the glowing liquid into stone moulds to make axes, blades, mirrors and bowls. Whoever controlled the supply of bronze controlled the best tools and weapons of the age, and that gave them great power over others.

Tin is a rare metal, found in only a handful of places, and the cities that wanted bronze had to import it across hundreds of miles of rivers, deserts and mountains. This created trade routes that linked distant regions, and it meant that a ruler's power could depend on the goodwill of merchants who lived far beyond his borders. The Bronze Age was, in that sense, an age of connection, in which no great power could stand entirely alone.

Iron ore is far more plentiful than copper or tin, and once smiths had learned to work it, about 3,200 years ago, iron tools became cheap enough for ordinary people. Farmers could now buy a stronger plough blade, an axe that held its edge and a sickle that cut cleanly through the stalks. Cheaper tools raised the size of the harvest, and a bigger harvest fed more people, more workers and more towns than ever before.

Chinese ironworkers learned to heat iron until it melted and then pour it into moulds as early as about twenty-five centuries ago, a technique that Europe would not use on a large scale until the late Middle Ages. Cast iron provided ploughshares, cooking pots and everyday tools for millions of Chinese farmers and their families. It is a useful warning that, for much of history, China was ahead of Europe in practical technology, and nothing about the future was fixed.

The first coins in the Mediterranean world were minted in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, about twenty-six centuries ago, and China developed its own soon afterwards. A small piece of metal stamped by the ruler was easy to carry, simple to count and accepted by strangers, so that trade no longer depended on swapping one good for another. Money is a quiet invention, yet it greases the wheels of every economy, from a village market to a great modern bank.

From about twenty-one centuries ago, caravans of camels and horses carried silk, spices, silver and glass along a web of routes that we now call the Silk Roads. These paths joined China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean world, though few traders ever travelled the whole way and goods usually passed through many hands. What moved along them was never only goods, for ideas and fashions went too.

Along these routes wheat moved east to China, while millet and rice moved west and south, and new foods enriched the diet of many lands. Indian mathematicians developed a system of numerals that included the zero, and it passed through the Arab world to Europe, where it eventually replaced the clumsy Roman figures. Few inventions have done more for science, trade and everyday arithmetic than that humble little circle, which stands for nothing at all.

Paper was being made in China about two thousand years ago, from rags, bark and old fishing nets, and it was far cheaper than silk or animal skin as a surface for writing. The skill spread slowly westward along the trade routes, reaching the Islamic world in the eighth century and Europe several centuries after that. A cheap and light material for making books made it far easier for knowledge to spread, and for more people to learn to read.

Merchants, monks and wandering scholars carried religions, stories and skills along the roads as faithfully as they carried silk. Buddhism travelled from India into China and beyond, and the Greek, Persian and Indian traditions of mathematics and medicine mingled in the cities of the Middle East. A traveller of those days could meet the whole world at a single inn.

Trade brought wealth, but it also carried danger, because germs travel as easily as goods do. Great epidemics sometimes followed the merchants along the caravan roads and the shipping lanes, killing people in cities that had never seen the disease before. One of the worst of them, in the fourteenth century, would help to change the balance of power in Europe.

Before railways and lorries, moving heavy goods overland was slow and ruinously expensive, whereas a single ship could carry as much as hundreds of carts and needed no road at all. Peoples with access to the sea, or to a navigable river, could therefore trade far more cheaply than those in the interior. Geography, in that sense, set the price of doing business, and some lands were simply born with cheaper roads than others.

The Mediterranean Sea sits between Europe, Africa and Asia, and for thousands of years it acted as a highway rather than a barrier. Phoenician sailors from the coast of the Levant and Greek sailors from the Aegean traded across it and founded colonies on its distant shores. Ideas, alphabets and crops travelled with the ships, and cities grew rich on the exchange.

At its height the Roman Empire controlled the entire Mediterranean coastline, and its soldiers, officials and merchants moved freely along its roads and shipping lanes. Grain from Egypt and North Africa fed the great city of Rome, which was one of the largest cities of the ancient world. For several centuries, a single government kept this enormous trading area stable and fairly safe.

The western half of the Roman Empire collapsed in the year 476, and without a central government the roads decayed, the coasts became less safe and long-distance trade shrank. Many cities in western Europe lost most of their people, and a patchwork of local rulers replaced the old imperial order. The eastern half of the empire survived for almost another thousand years, with its splendid capital at Constantinople.

In the Indian Ocean the monsoon winds blow from one direction in summer and the opposite direction in winter, which allowed sailors to make dependable round trips of thousands of miles. Boats with triangular sails carried cloth, spices, pearls and porcelain between East Africa, Arabia, India and China for more than a thousand years. Nobody ruled this ocean, yet it carried more trade than any other body of water.

Along the East African coast a string of Swahili trading cities, such as Kilwa and Mombasa, grew rich by acting as go-betweens in the Indian Ocean. They sold gold and ivory from the interior and bought cloth, beads and fine porcelain from India and China, building stone houses and mosques with the profits. Africa was therefore an active and wealthy partner in the trade of the whole world, and not merely a distant bystander.

Under the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago, Chinese shipyards produced large vessels with watertight compartments and several masts, and sailors steered with the help of the magnetic compass. At home, merchants began to use paper money, which was lighter and safer to carry than strings of copper coins. China was then probably one of the most commercial and technically skilled societies on Earth, and certainly one of the richest.

Camel caravans carried salt, cloth and copper south across the Sahara and brought back West African gold, which was needed in every mint of the Mediterranean world. The empire of Mali grew powerful on this trade, and its ruler Mansa Musa made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 so lavishly that his spending was said to have lowered the price of gold in Cairo for years. The cities of Timbuktu and Gao, on the edge of the desert, became famous centres of trade and learning for many generations.

Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific Ocean in double-hulled canoes, steering by the stars, the swell of the waves and the flight of birds. Over many centuries they settled islands from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the south, which they reached only about seven hundred years ago. It remains one of the greatest feats of exploration in human history, and it was achieved without a single written map.

By about the year 1000, a vast web of trade routes bound together Asia, Africa and Europe, and the busiest, richest nodes of that web lay in the Middle East, India and China. Western Europe sat on its far edge, sending mostly timber, wool, slaves and furs in exchange for luxuries. Nobody looking at the map then could have guessed that the next five hundred years would change the picture.

Gunpowder, the magnetic compass and printing were all first developed in China, and they reached Europe through the networks of trade and war that crossed Asia. European craftsmen studied them, copied them and then improved them, often in ways that suited their own rivalries and markets. Borrowing, in the history of technology, is far more common than inventing from nothing.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith in the German city of Mainz, built a printing press that used movable metal letters, which could be set in any order and used again. Because European languages are written with a small alphabet, the method worked extremely well, and within a few decades presses were operating in hundreds of towns. Books fell sharply in price, and knowledge became a good that ordinary people could afford.

Europe was never a single empire but a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies and free cities, divided from one another by mountains, rivers, forests and stretches of sea. The long coastline and jagged peninsulas made it hard for any one ruler to conquer everything, even though many tried. China, in contrast, had broad plains and two great rivers, and was usually unified under one government.

Because Europe's rulers were always in rivalry, each needed money, soldiers and skilled advisers, and each had a reason to welcome talent that another king had turned away. An inventor, a banker or a preacher who was not welcome in one country could simply cross the border and try again somewhere else. Some historians believe that this competition, more than any single invention, helped Europe's ideas survive.

In 1521 the German preacher Martin Luther, whose writings challenged the Church, was declared an outlaw by the emperor and might have been silenced. A local prince, the Elector of Saxony, gave him shelter instead, and the printing presses of many cities spread his arguments across Europe within a few years. In a more tightly unified state, a single order might have ended the matter.

Christopher Columbus spent years trying to persuade rulers to pay for a voyage westward across the Atlantic, and he was turned away by Portugal and by other courts before the monarchs of Spain finally agreed in 1492. A continent with only one court would have offered only one chance, and a single refusal would have ended the project. Europe's many rivals, by accident, gave bold ideas many different doors on which to knock.

Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming emperors sent enormous fleets under Admiral Zheng He to India, Arabia and the coast of East Africa, with ships larger than any in Europe. Then the court brought the voyages to a halt, and the great ships were allowed to decay. Historians still argue about why, and some say that the fleets were never meant to make a profit in the first place.

A single government can keep the peace over a huge territory, build canals and roads, and create a vast market, and China enjoyed those benefits for long periods. It can also halt a promising idea with one decision, whereas a divided continent finds it harder to stop everything at once. Disunity, though, brought Europe war after war, so there is no simple rule to learn here.

In Italy the independent cities of Venice, Genoa and Florence grew rich by trading with the eastern Mediterranean, and their bankers lent money across Europe. Merchants developed careful double-entry bookkeeping, which allowed them to see at a glance whether a venture was making a profit or a loss. Business methods that sound dull proved to be among the most powerful tools that Europe ever developed, and they were soon copied elsewhere.

In the twelfth century and after, scholars in cities such as Toledo, in Spain, translated Arabic books of mathematics, medicine and philosophy into Latin, and they passed them on to the universities of Europe. The ideas of Greece, India and Persia reached Western readers largely through this channel. Europe, in short, was a student of the wider world for centuries before it became a teacher.

Portugal sits on the Atlantic edge of Europe, and in the fifteenth century its sailors began creeping down the coast of Africa, a little farther south each year. They were searching for gold, for allies and, above all, for a sea route to the rich markets of Asia. Prince Henry, who paid for many of these voyages, never sailed far himself, but he made exploration a national project.

Portuguese shipbuilders developed the caravel, a light and handy vessel with triangular sails that could sail close to the wind, an idea borrowed from Arab ships. With the compass, the astrolabe for measuring the height of the sun and stars, and charts that improved with every voyage, sailors could now risk the open ocean. Each of these tools had come from somewhere else, and Europe's skill was in putting them together.

In 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias was driven by storms around the southern tip of Africa, and he realised that the coast now turned northeast into the Indian Ocean. His exhausted crew persuaded him to turn back, but he had shown that a route from the Atlantic to Asia by sea was possible. The cape was later named the Cape of Good Hope, in honour of that promise.

In August 1492 Christopher Columbus left Spain with three small ships and sailed west across the Atlantic, convinced that he would reach Asia. After about ten weeks at sea, his crew sighted an island in the Bahamas, and the voyage that he had planned as a shortcut to India instead opened the way to two continents that Europeans had not known. Columbus himself believed until the end of his life that he had reached the edge of the Indies in Asia.

In 1498 Vasco da Gama of Portugal followed the route that Dias had begun, rounded Africa, crossed the Indian Ocean with the help of a local pilot and arrived at the port of Calicut in India. He returned with a cargo of pepper and other spices that sold for far more than the cost of the whole voyage. Portugal had found a way into the richest trade in the world, and other European nations were eager to follow its example.

Europeans wanted pepper, silk, porcelain and gold, and the kings who competed for them hoped to avoid the middlemen who took a share at every stage. Asian merchants, however, had little interest in the woollen cloth and simple tools that Europe produced, so the Europeans had to pay in silver and gold. This was a poor trading position, and it made the new sea routes more attractive.

In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan sailed from Spain with five ships and about two hundred and fifty men, hoping to reach the Spice Islands by heading west. He was killed in the Philippines in 1521, but one battered ship under Juan Sebastian Elcano completed the journey in 1522, carrying fewer than twenty men. It was the first voyage around the entire globe, and it proved to everyone that the oceans of the world were joined together.

Portuguese ships were armed with heavy cannon, and in the early sixteenth century they used them to seize ports such as Goa in India and Malacca on the strait between Malaysia and Sumatra. They controlled a string of harbours and took a share of the spice trade, yet they were far too few to conquer the great land empires of Asia. At sea, however, they had gained an edge that would last for a very long time, and it would be used again and again.

In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed on the coast of Mexico with about five hundred Spanish soldiers, and within two years the Aztec Empire had fallen. The Spaniards could not have won alone, since thousands of local allies who resented Aztec rule fought beside them, and a deadly smallpox epidemic killed many defenders of the capital, Tenochtitlan. The conquest was the work of local alliances, disease and weapons together, and not of Spanish soldiers alone.

In 1532 Francisco Pizarro, leading fewer than two hundred Spaniards, captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca in the Andes and held him for ransom. The Inca Empire had just been shaken by a bitter civil war and by smallpox, which had spread ahead of the Spaniards and probably killed the previous emperor. Once again, a handful of men succeeded because the ground had already been prepared.

When Europeans crossed the Atlantic, they carried with them smallpox, measles and influenza, diseases against which the peoples of the Americas had no inherited defences. Millions fell ill and died in outbreaks that sometimes raced ahead of the newcomers themselves. It was one of the greatest human catastrophes in all of history, and it began almost at once.

In an epidemic that strikes everyone at the same time, there is nobody left to nurse the sick, carry water or tend the fields. Hunger followed disease, and people weakened by hunger died more easily, so each wave of illness made the next one deadlier. Whole villages were abandoned, and their histories, languages and customs vanished with them in many cases.

Nobody counted the dead, and so the estimates that historians give differ widely, from a few million to many tens of millions. Most scholars agree, though, that the population of the Americas fell by a very large share, perhaps by the majority, within about a century of first contact. The exact figure is still disputed among scholars, but the terrible scale of the loss is not in doubt.

With so many people gone, kingdoms lost their armies, their farmers and their leaders, and fields that had been cultivated for centuries were left empty. Europeans took the land, first as conquerors and later as settlers, and they met far less resistance than they would have faced a century earlier. Disease did not cause the conquest on its own, but it made it enormously easier.

In 1545 the Spaniards found a mountain of silver at Potosi, in the Andes of present-day Bolivia, and for generations its mines made the Spanish crown richer than any in Europe. The work was done largely by Indigenous labourers who were forced into the mines under a harsh system of compulsory service, and many died there. The silver they dug flowed to Spain, and then on to merchants in Europe and China.

After 1492 a vast exchange of plants, animals and germs began between the Americas and the rest of the world, which historians call the Columbian Exchange. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, chillies and cacao travelled east across the ocean, while wheat, sugar, cattle, pigs and horses travelled west. Almost every kitchen and farm in the world was changed by it, and the meals that we eat today still show its effects.

The potato thrived in the cool, damp climate of northern Europe and provided more calories per acre than the grains that farmers had grown before. Families could now feed themselves on a smaller plot, so more land was freed for other crops, and the population of Europe rose. Some historians think this extra food helped to power the growth of cities and, later, of industry.

American crops did not stop in Europe, for maize and cassava spread across Africa and became staple foods in many regions. In China, sweet potatoes and maize could be grown on hillsides that were too poor for rice, which helped the population to climb. A few seeds carried across an ocean had changed what the world could eat.

Europe gained land, silver, new crops and a new range of markets from the Americas, and those gains helped to enrich its merchants and rulers. The Indigenous peoples of the Americas paid for them with their lives, their lands and in many cases their freedom. It is hard to tell the story of Europe's rise honestly without telling the other half.

The peoples of the Americas did not vanish, and it would be a serious mistake to write of them only as victims. Millions of their descendants live today, speaking languages such as Quechua, Nahuatl and Maya, farming the same mountainsides and keeping old traditions alive. Their survival is a story of courage that is still being written, and the next chapter shows how Europe's new lands came to be worked.

Europeans developed a craving for sugar, which was sweet, durable and valuable, and from the sixteenth century planters in Brazil and the Caribbean set up huge plantations to grow it. Sugar cane was brutally hard to cut and to boil down, and the estates wanted a large and cheap supply of labour. The search for that labour led, step by step, to one of the greatest crimes in the history of the world.

With so many Indigenous workers dead, and European servants too few and too expensive, planters turned to traders who bought and sold enslaved Africans. Slavery had existed in many societies for thousands of years, but the Atlantic trade was larger, more commercial and more cruel than almost anything before it. European merchants and shippers ran it, with the help of some African rulers who sold captives.

Between the early sixteenth century and the 1860s, more than twelve million people were taken from Africa and loaded onto ships bound for the Americas. Historians who have counted the records of the voyages believe that well over ten million of them reached the other shore alive. Behind each number was a person with a name, a family and a home that they never saw again.

The journey across the Atlantic, known as the Middle Passage, could last many weeks, during which captives were chained below deck in tightly packed rows with little food, water or air. Disease spread quickly in such conditions, and many people died before they ever saw land. Captives resisted whenever they could, and revolts on board the ships were not rare.

On the plantations enslaved men, women and children worked from dawn until dark, without wages and under the threat of punishment, cutting cane, tending the boilers or picking cotton. The law of the colonies treated them as property to be bought, sold and inherited, and families were often broken up by sales. Despite all of this, they preserved songs, languages, faiths and a stubborn dignity that the system could never take away.

Sugar was only the first of the plantation crops, and tobacco, rice, coffee and, above all, cotton were soon grown by enslaved labour as well. In the American South the number of enslaved people rose to almost four million by 1860, and cotton became the nation's most valuable export. A large part of the early industrial world was supplied by workers who were never paid.

Ports such as Bristol, Liverpool, Lisbon and Nantes grew rich on the trade in people and in the goods that they produced, and merchants invested their profits in banks, insurance and new businesses. Historians still debate how large a share of Europe's growth came from slavery, since some argue that it was central and others that it was only a part of a larger story. What nobody disputes is that it brought wealth to some and ruin to others.

The slave trade removed millions of people from Africa, mostly young adults, and it encouraged raids and wars in which captives were taken to be sold. A few kingdoms grew powerful by supplying the trade, but whole regions lost their young people, their security and their trust. Some economists find that the places most heavily affected remain poorer today, although this is still being studied.

In 1791 the enslaved people of the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in revolt, led in part by Toussaint Louverture, and in 1804 they declared their country independent as Haiti. It was the first nation in the Americas to be founded by formerly enslaved people. In 1825, France demanded a heavy payment in return for recognising Haiti, a debt that took more than a century to repay and that held its economy back.

Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and abolished slavery in most of its colonies in 1833, after long campaigns by formerly enslaved people, ordinary citizens and religious reformers. The government paid enormous compensation to the owners, but nothing to the people who had been enslaved. Slavery ended in the United States in 1865 and in Brazil in 1888, and the wounds of the system are felt to this day.

Britain was fortunate to sit on large deposits of coal, and much of it lay close to the surface or close to rivers and ports, where it could be dug and shipped cheaply. In the eighteenth century this accident of geology gave British workshops a source of heat that was the envy of other countries. Place, in this story, did matter a great deal, though as we shall see it did not act alone.

Over the centuries Britain's forests had been felled for building, shipbuilding and fuel, and by the seventeenth century wood was scarce and costly. People turned to coal to heat their houses and to fire their forges, and London became a city that ran on it. Cheap energy is a hidden ingredient of wealth, and Britain had a great deal of it.

As the shallow seams ran out and miners dug deeper, water seeped into the tunnels, and some mines flooded so badly that work had to stop. Pumps worked by teams of horses were slow, costly and weak, so mine owners offered a rich reward to anyone who could pump more cheaply. Necessity, as so often in history, called out an invention, and the inventors were not slow to answer the call.

In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine that could pump water from a mine, and soon dozens of them were working in the coalfields. It used enormous quantities of coal, which would have made it too costly almost anywhere else, but at the mouth of a coal mine fuel was practically free. This was a case in which the right tool turned up in the right place.

In the 1760s James Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, worked out that Newcomen's engine wasted much of its heat by cooling and reheating the same cylinder, and he added a separate condenser. His design used far less coal, and with his partner Matthew Boulton he later adapted it to turn wheels, so that the steam engine could drive machines as well as pumps. A sound idea needed a good partner and a good market, and Watt, unusually, found both of them in the same city.

Fine, bright cotton cloth from India, known as calico, was a sensation in Europe, for it was lighter, washable and cheaper than wool. British merchants wanted to compete and they protected their own makers with laws, but what they needed was a way of making cotton cloth in quantity at low cost. The answer would come from machines, and from the clever men who built them, and not from cheaper labour alone.

In the 1760s and 1770s a series of inventions, including the spinning jenny, the water frame and the mule, multiplied the amount of thread that a single worker could spin. Their makers were mostly practical men, such as James Hargreaves, Richard Arkwright and Samuel Crompton, who tinkered with ideas until they worked. The result was cotton thread in quantities that earlier spinners could hardly have imagined.

Machines were soon gathered under a single roof in large mills, powered first by water and later by steam, and the town of Manchester became known as Cottonopolis. The cloth poured out cheaply and was sold across the world, but the raw cotton came largely from plantations in the Americas worked by enslaved people. Industrial wealth and slavery were bound together in the same chain of trade, and that is an uncomfortable fact of this history.

Life in the early factories was hard, with days of twelve hours or more, little pay, deafening noise and moving machinery that could maim a careless worker. Children worked in the mills alongside adults, and the crowded industrial towns around them were filthy and unhealthy. Laws such as the Factory Act of 1833 began to limit the hours of the youngest workers, but wages and conditions improved only slowly.

Historians still argue about why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain rather than in China, India or elsewhere in Europe. Some emphasise its cheap coal and relatively high wages, which made machines worth building, while others stress its empire and trade, its habit of practical experiment, or its laws and government. The honest answer is very probably a combination, and the weights are still disputed.

Nobody builds a workshop, plants an orchard or lends money unless they believe that they will be allowed to keep the rewards. Fair courts, enforceable contracts and secure property turn that hope into confidence, and confidence leads to investment. Many economists think that the quality of a country's rules is among the most important causes of its wealth.

Where a ruler could seize a merchant's goods at will, tax without limit or simply refuse to repay a loan, sensible people hid their wealth and avoided risk. In the 1340s King Edward III of England defaulted on his debts to Italian bankers, and two of the greatest banking houses of Florence collapsed. Lenders learned, at great cost, that a king who answers to nobody is a very dangerous person to lend money to.

In the 1640s a civil war broke out in England between King Charles I, who wished to rule and tax without consulting anyone, and a Parliament determined to defend its rights. The king lost the war and in 1649 he was put on trial and executed, which astonished and horrified much of Europe. Monarchy was soon restored, but the old claim of unlimited royal power never fully recovered.

In 1688 a group of English leaders invited the Dutch prince William of Orange and his wife Mary to take the throne in what became known as the Glorious Revolution, and the old king fled. The Bill of Rights of 1689 declared that the monarch could not make laws, raise taxes or keep an army in peacetime without the consent of Parliament. These changes did not create a democracy, but they placed real limits on royal power.

Because Parliament controlled the taxes and had pledged to repay the government's debts, lenders came to trust the British state, and it could borrow at lower rates than its rivals. The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to help manage that borrowing, and over the next century the money raised paid for a powerful navy. Trust, it turns out, can be as useful to a government as gold, and far cheaper to produce than a silver mine.

It would be wrong to suppose that the new rules served everybody equally, because only a small minority of men had the vote and women had none. Landowners in the eighteenth century fenced off common land that poor villagers had used for generations, and they could do so legally, since they made the laws. Secure property was a powerful engine of growth, but it was not secure for everyone.

In 1624 an English law gave inventors the right to hold a patent, a temporary monopoly on their invention, and it rewarded them for the effort and risk of developing it. Patents also required inventors to describe their ideas publicly, so that others could study and later improve them. Watt's partnership with Boulton relied on such protection, though patents also sometimes slowed progress, since they gave their holders a means of blocking rivals.

In the early seventeenth century, companies such as the Dutch East India Company and the English East India Company sold shares to many investors, who shared the cost of risky overseas ventures and the profits that followed. Insurance, arranged in London coffee houses and elsewhere, paid out if a ship was lost at sea, and so made sailing less of a gamble. Some of these great companies also used armies, forts and violence to build trading monopolies.

The Dutch Republic was probably the richest country in Europe in the seventeenth century, thanks to its merchants, its efficient banks and the world's first lasting stock exchange in Amsterdam. Its towns tolerated people of many faiths, attracted skilled refugees and governed themselves through councils in which merchants had a say. The Dutch showed that a small, watery country with few natural resources could thrive on good institutions.

Spain received huge flows of American silver, yet its crown spent more on wars than it received, borrowed heavily and defaulted on its debts several times in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Its rulers had little reason to respect the property of merchants and had few checks on their spending. Rules are made by people in particular circumstances, which means that they can also be changed by people who decide to change them.

In 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in the north of England, and it became the first public railway in the world to use steam locomotives. George Stephenson's engine pulled wagons of coal along iron rails, and soon afterwards passengers began to ride as well. Within a few years his line between Liverpool and Manchester had shown that rail travel could be both fast and profitable.

Railways cut the cost and time of moving goods so sharply that farmers could sell fresh milk, fish and vegetables to cities a hundred miles away. Small local markets merged into national ones, firms could specialise and serve far more customers, and towns along the line grew quickly. Britain even adopted a single time across the country, because railway timetables could not work otherwise.

The electric telegraph, which spread from the 1840s, carried news in minutes instead of days, and steamships began to cross the oceans on regular schedules, whatever the wind. A cable laid under the Atlantic joined Europe and America in 1866, and merchants could suddenly learn the price of cotton or wheat on the far side of the world. Distance, which had always been the great enemy of trade and of news, was shrinking faster than anyone had expected.

Other countries were eager to copy the new machines, and for some time Britain tried to ban the export of its machinery and the departure of its skilled workers. It could not enforce the laws for long, and engineers, drawings and ideas spread across the sea regardless. Samuel Slater, a young mill worker who memorised the design of a spinning frame, opened a cotton mill in Rhode Island in 1790.

Belgium was the first country on the European mainland to industrialise on the British pattern, with coal and iron ore conveniently close to one another. An English-born engineer, John Cockerill, set up huge ironworks and machine factories, and the new government built one of the first railway networks on the continent. A small country with few resources had shown that the British recipe for industry could be copied and adapted elsewhere.

Germany and the United States soon built great industries of their own, with their wide lands, rich coal and iron, and growing markets. German states removed tariffs between them in a customs union that began in 1834, while Americans built canals, then railways, until a line joined the two coasts in 1869. Neither country had to start from nothing, because both could learn from Britain, and both did so with great energy and skill.

Countries that built schools and universities gained engineers, chemists, clerks and skilled workers who could understand a machine and improve it. Prussia, the largest German state, had made school attendance compulsory in the eighteenth century, and German universities pioneered laboratory science, especially in chemistry. Education was not a luxury that followed wealth, for it was one of the roads that led to it.

From the middle of the nineteenth century cheap steel, electric power and a stream of new chemicals gave birth to what is often called the second industrial revolution. Germany and the United States led it, since they had invested heavily in science and technical education, and Britain's early lead began to fade. Being first, it seems, was no guarantee of staying first, since later arrivals could learn from the leader and sometimes overtake it.

A country that starts late can borrow ideas that others have already tested and avoid the costly mistakes of the pioneers, which is sometimes called the advantage of backwardness. To take advantage, though, a country needs educated workers, secure rules and enough money to import machines, and many countries lacked at least one of these. Copying a technology is easier than inventing it, but it is far from effortless.

Switzerland, with its mountains, its lack of a coastline and its absence of coal, looked an unlikely candidate for industrial success. Its people harnessed the power of fast streams, trained skilled workers in watchmaking and engineering, and built banks and insurers that gained a worldwide reputation for reliability. The Swiss case shows that geography can be overcome by determination, education and trustworthy rules.

Two centuries ago almost everyone on Earth was poor by modern standards, and ordinary life was short and precarious. In much of the world about one child in three died before the age of five, and an adult might be carried off by a fever, an infected cut or a bad harvest. Wealth and health were never really separate stories, for in the centuries that followed they rose together and fed one another.

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught the mild disease cowpox seemed protected from smallpox, and he tested the idea by inoculating a young boy. The word vaccine comes from the Latin for cow, vacca, and the method spread around the world over the following decades. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox, once one of humanity's worst killers, had been wiped out.

In 1854 an outbreak of cholera killed hundreds of people in a single district of London, and a doctor named John Snow marked the cases on a map and found that they clustered around one public water pump. When the handle was removed, the outbreak faded, and Snow's evidence helped to persuade doubters that dirty water, rather than bad air, spread the disease. Within a few decades, scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch had shown that germs were the true cause.

After the foul summer of 1858, known as the Great Stink, the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a vast system of brick sewers beneath London that carried waste away from the river. Cities across Europe and North America followed, laying pipes to bring clean water in and take dirty water out, and deaths from cholera and typhoid fell steeply. Such unglamorous public works have probably saved more lives than almost any single miracle drug, though few people ever think to thank the engineers.

A healthy child misses fewer days of school and learns more, and a healthy adult can work harder and for more years of life. Better health therefore helped to make countries richer, and richer countries could afford more doctors, hospitals and clean water, in a cycle that fed itself. Once the cycle started, it was difficult for those left outside it to catch up.

The average person on Earth in 1800 could expect to live about thirty years, a figure pulled down by the huge number of children who died young. Today the world average is above seventy, one of the greatest achievements in human history, although a baby born in the poorest countries can still expect a markedly shorter life. The gap in health is among the clearest signs of the gap in wealth.

Around 1800 only about one adult in eight in the entire world could read and write, and most children never saw the inside of a school. Over two centuries, governments, churches, charities and parents built schools, and today roughly nine adults in ten can read. Literacy turned out to be both a cause and a result of growth, because educated people invent, organise and earn more.

When parents could be confident that their children would survive, families gradually began to have fewer babies and to invest more in the health and schooling of each one. Economists call this the demographic transition, and it has happened in country after country as incomes and health have improved. Smaller families, better educated children and more working adults helped to speed up growth.

For thousands of years the average person's income hardly rose at all, so that a peasant in the year 1500 lived not much better than one in the year 500. After about 1800 incomes began to climb rapidly in a few countries, while in others they rose slowly or not at all, and the gap that opened is called the Great Divergence. It is one of the strangest and most important facts in the whole of economic history, and economists still argue about its causes.

Around 1800 the richest countries were, by most estimates, perhaps three or four times richer than the poorest, which is a real difference but not an enormous one. Today the richest countries are dozens of times richer than the poorest, so that the gap has multiplied several times over in just two centuries. The challenge for this book, therefore, is to explain a change that happened fast, and that has been unevenly spread.

In 1868 a group of Japanese leaders overthrew the old order and began the Meiji period, determined to catch up with the Western powers before they were swallowed by them. They sent missions of officials to Europe and America to study factories, schools and governments, then came home and copied what they had seen. Japan was one of the few Asian countries that stayed independent while it industrialised.

Within a few years the Meiji government made primary schooling compulsory, opened a railway between Tokyo and Yokohama in 1872 and set up banks, factories and a modern postal service. It hired foreign engineers and teachers for a time, but trained Japanese workers to take their places as soon as possible. Learning was a national project in which almost everyone took part, from the emperor's ministers to the village schoolmaster.

Japan's success had a darker side, for the new state built a powerful army and navy and used them to take territory from its neighbours. It seized Taiwan in 1895 and annexed Korea in 1910, and it later led its people into a ruinous war that caused immense suffering across Asia. Industrial strength can be used for good or ill, and wealth tells us nothing about wisdom.

From the 1950s onward four East Asian economies, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong, grew at astonishing speed and became known as the Asian tigers. They invested heavily in schools, encouraged exports and made the most of cheap, hard-working labour that was steadily becoming more skilled. In a single lifetime they moved from poverty to wealth that had taken Europe centuries to achieve.

Before they industrialised, South Korea and Taiwan carried out land reforms in the late 1940s and 1950s that broke up large estates and gave farmers their own plots. Families who owned their land worked it harder, saved more and sent their children to school, and the powerful landlord class lost its grip on politics. A fairer start made the later boom both faster and broader, since more families could join in and share the gains.

Singapore is a tiny island with almost no natural resources, no farmland to speak of and not even its own water supply. After independence in 1965 it built one of the world's busiest ports, welcomed foreign firms, kept its courts and civil service honest and invested in schools. Within a generation its people had become as rich as those of many older industrial nations.

After 1978 the Chinese government, led by Deng Xiaoping, began to let farmers sell their surplus crops and opened special zones on the coast to foreign investment. Factories multiplied, exports soared and, by the standards the World Bank uses, hundreds of millions of Chinese people rose out of extreme poverty in a few decades. It was among the fastest reductions in poverty that the world has ever recorded, though it came with many costs of its own.

India began to free its economy from heavy controls in 1991, and its growth speeded up, particularly in software, services and some kinds of manufacturing. Millions of people moved out of poverty and a large middle class emerged, although millions more remain poor and many struggle without good schools or healthcare. Catching up is rarely quick, smooth or complete, and India's long road is a good example of that truth.

Several African countries have also grown quickly in recent decades, among them Botswana and the island nation of Mauritius. Botswana used the income from its diamond mines sensibly, with fairly honest courts and steady rules, while Mauritius moved from sugar to textiles, tourism and financial services. Their stories show that no people is born unable to succeed, and that good rules and sensible choices can matter a great deal.

There is no single recipe that works in every country, and some governments that followed fashionable advice found that it failed in their own circumstances. Nevertheless, the countries that caught up usually had schools, public health, openness to trade, a measure of peace and a government that could do its job. The gap between rich and poor nations is real, but it is not fixed.

A landlocked country has no port of its own, so its exports and imports must cross the territory of neighbours, paying fees and enduring delays at every border. Studies find that such countries tend to grow more slowly than those with a coast, particularly when their neighbours are poor or unstable. Yet Switzerland, Austria and Luxembourg are landlocked and rich, which tells us that geography raises a hurdle without building a wall.

Malaria, which is spread by the bite of a mosquito, still kills hundreds of thousands of people every year, and most of its victims are young children in sub-Saharan Africa. The illness also keeps children away from school and adults away from work, and it discourages investors and visitors from entering affected regions. It is a disease of poverty that also helps to cause poverty, and so it is a trap that is very hard to escape.

In large parts of tropical Africa, the bite of the tsetse fly spreads a disease that kills cattle and horses and also sickens people. Farmers in these regions could not easily keep the animals that pulled ploughs and carts in Europe and Asia, so that they missed out on the extra food and the manure that animals provide. Place can shape a people's farming, and so their food and their wealth, in ways that nobody ever chose for themselves.

In 1884 and 1885 the European powers met in Berlin to agree on rules for dividing up Africa among themselves, and no African ruler was invited to the conference. The borders that they drew on their maps often cut through kingdoms and language groups, and joined together peoples who had never shared a government. By 1914 almost the whole continent was under European control, and only a very few countries still governed themselves.

In many colonies the rulers built railways that ran from mines and plantations straight to the nearest port, rather than linking one local town to another. Raw materials such as cotton, rubber, copper and cocoa were shipped abroad, where the factories and the profits were, and little was spent on schools or on local industry. Such an economy was designed to serve the colonising country first and the colony second.

India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, Ghana in 1957, and in 1960 alone seventeen African countries won their freedom. The new states faced enormous challenges, since they often had few trained doctors, engineers or civil servants and borders that had been drawn by outsiders. Independence was a great moral victory, but it was only the beginning of the work of building a prosperous country.

A civil war destroys more than buildings, for it wrecks roads, schools and farms, drives away investors and breeds a suspicion between neighbours that can last for generations. Economists find that a long conflict can set a country back by decades, and that countries that have fought one war are more likely to fight another. Peace is the first and cheapest investment in growth, even though it is not the most exciting.

Natural riches such as oil and diamonds can bring huge sums of money, and yet in some countries they seem to have brought only corruption, conflict and neglect of everything else. Rulers who live on income from a mine or a well need not tax their people, and so they have less reason to listen to them or to build schools. This is sometimes called the resource curse, although Norway and Botswana have shown that it can be avoided.

Many poor countries borrowed heavily in the 1970s and then found that their debts grew impossible to repay when interest rates rose and commodity prices fell. Their farmers also faced the problem of wildly swinging prices for crops such as coffee, and the rich countries protected their own farmers with subsidies and tariffs. Economists disagree about how much of the blame lies abroad, and how much lies in the policies and the rulers of the poor countries themselves.

Every wall that has been described is real, but none of them has proved impossible to climb, and poor countries can sometimes leap ahead by adopting a new technology without building the old one first. In Kenya a money service called M-Pesa, launched in 2007, allowed people to send and receive payments on a simple mobile phone, and it quickly spread to millions of customers who had never had a bank account. Such innovations are a reason for hope, because they show that the past does not have to be repeated exactly by every country.

In 1347 trading ships arriving in Sicily from the Black Sea brought with them the plague that came to be called the Black Death. Over the next few years it spread through almost every country in Europe, killing a very large share of the population, perhaps a third or more. Nobody planned it, and nobody could have prevented it, which is exactly what makes it a matter of chance.

With so many people dead, labour became scarce, and landowners who needed their fields worked had to offer better wages and easier terms. In much of western Europe the old bonds that tied peasants to their lords weakened, although in some regions of eastern Europe, rulers tightened their grip instead. Historians still debate how far this one disaster shaped the long-term differences between regions.

History is full of accidents, and some of them may have mattered a great deal. In 1588 a Spanish fleet sent to invade England was harried by English ships and then battered by storms, and its defeat helped to preserve England's independence. Nobody can say for certain what would have followed had it succeeded, but it is a reminder that the course of events is never entirely fixed.

War destroys homes, factories, bridges and the trust that people have in one another, and in 1945 the cities of Germany and Japan lay in ruins. Within a few decades both countries had recovered and become two of the richest in the world, helped in part by American aid and by a long period of peace. What had survived was the thing that matters most: skilled, educated people who knew how to build.

No people is naturally cleverer, more hard-working or more inventive than another, and the history of this book shows why. At different times the lead in science, wealth and technology has belonged to Mesopotamia, China, the Islamic world, Italy, the Netherlands and Britain, and none of them was born with a special gift. Any child, raised in a place with good schools and good health, can learn to do almost anything.

Economists agree on a good deal more than outsiders often suppose, for almost all of them accept that peace, good health, widespread schooling, honest courts and open trade help countries to grow. They still argue fiercely about how much each factor matters, in what order they should come and what governments should do when they are missing. The disagreement is a sign of a living science, and not of a failed one, since good scholars should always test each other's ideas.

Place gave some peoples a head start, through the crops and animals that they could farm, the coasts that they could sail from and the coal that lay under their feet. Rules decided how well that head start was used, since good courts, fair laws and stable governments encouraged people to invest and invent, and chance added accident and surprise at every stage. The three work together like gears, and none of them explains the whole story alone.

Unlike a scientist in a laboratory, a historian cannot rerun the past with one ingredient removed to see what happens, so every neat explanation of the world's wealth should be held with a measure of caution. The honest conclusion is that many causes acted together, that some of them are still unknown and that the weight of each one is still argued over. A single clever theory that explains everything should always be a reason for suspicion.

The ranking of the richest places has changed many times, and no leader has ever held on for ever. The cities of Mesopotamia and the courts of China gave way to the merchant republics of Italy, then to the Dutch, to Britain and to the United States, while Asia has been rising again in our own time. Anyone who thinks that the present order is permanent has not studied the past.

The league table of wealthy nations has been reshuffled many times, and it will certainly be reshuffled again. Poor countries are not condemned by their geography or their past, and a few of them have shown that the gap can be crossed within a lifetime. The question of why some countries got rich first is old, but the more useful question for our own time may be how many more can follow.
